documents.abstract: In many educational contexts, classroom disciplinary practices are often dominated by punitive approaches, in which mistakes are responded to criticism or punishment in the name of maintaining order and discipline. Such practices may discourage participation, reduce students’ confidence, and limit meaningful engagement, particularly in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning where students are already vulnerable to anxiety and fear of making mistakes. However, alternative approaches that emphasize support rather than punishment remain underexplored, especially in relation to their broader impact on classroom dynamics. Grounded in Behaviourist theory by Skinner, this study investigates whether and how Positive Reinforcement enhances student engagement in EFL classrooms. A sequential explanatory mixed-method design was employed involving 105 junior high school students in Indonesia. Quantitative data were collected through pre- and post-surveys, followed by qualitative interviews with five students to further explain the statistical findings. The quantitative results showed a statistically significant improvement in students’ engagement (p < .001) after the implementation of Positive Reinforcement, with a large effect size (r = 0.86), indicating a strong practical impact. The qualitative findings further revealed improvements in five major areas: (1) behavioural engagement, (2) cognitive engagement, (3) emotional safety and confidence, (4) peer interaction and communication, and (5) student-teacher relationships. These findings suggest that shifting from punitive to supportive practices not only enhances individual student engagement but also contributes to the development of more positive and supportive classroom dynamics in EFL learning environments.

Purpose This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can improve organizational crisis management as firms increasingly operate in a polycrisis marked by overlapping pandemics, geopolitical conflict and rapid technological change. It maps AI capabilities to the before, during and after phases of the crisis lifecycle. Design/methodology/approach This narrative/conceptual review synthesizes empirical and theoretical scholarship on AI in crisis management across management, information systems and crisis communication journals. It integrates evidence on early warning, anticipation, social media analytics, crisis communication and resilience into a lifecycle framework. Findings Before a crisis, AI-driven early warning systems can predict disruptions weeks in advance and help mitigate losses. During a crisis, natural language processing supports situational awareness, and generative AI accelerates communication. After a crisis, social listening and simulation support learning, while deepfake defense protects reputation. Benefits are conditional on governance maturity and complement, rather than replace, human judgment. Practical implications Firms should adopt AI proactively but judiciously for sensing, triage and rehearsal, guided by governance readiness rather than novelty. They should also invest in data governance and interoperability. Organizations should keep accountability and ethical judgment visibly human where trust and empathy matter most. SMEs benefit from modular, centrally supported adoption pathways. Originality/value This paper integrates AI and crisis management into a lifecycle framework centered on the governance conditions that enable AI to improve outcomes. It advances two propositions: (1) AI’s value shifts from augmenting anticipation to substituting risk as authorship becomes visible, and (2) governance maturity moderates, rather than predicts, AI’s crisis-management payoff.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: This chapter explores emerging trends and future innovations that are reshaping ESH Management Systems through the convergence of AI, robotics, the IoT, and advanced analytics. Building upon the PRIM governance framework developed throughout the book, this chapter demonstrates how these technologies are transforming ESH management from reactive, compliance-based processes into predictive, interconnected, and intelligent operational systems. It examines the role of IoT as the digital sensory system that continuously collects real-time operational and environmental data to support AI-driven analytics, predictive modeling, automation, and informed decision-making. This chapter also introduces Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) as a critical capability for improving transparency, trust, accountability, and human performance in safety-critical environments, illustrating how explainable AI strengthens human-in-the-loop (HITL) decision-making, regulatory defensibility, and organizational confidence in AI-supported recommendations. Finally, this chapter examines the policy, governance, and global implementation challenges associated with AI-enabled ESH Management Systems, emphasizing the importance of ethical principles, cybersecurity, data quality, human oversight, workforce trust, and internationally recognized governance practices. As AI technologies continue to evolve faster than regulatory frameworks, organizations are encouraged to develop adaptive governance systems that balance innovation with responsible implementation. Collectively, these emerging technologies and governance principles position AI as a strategic enabler of safer workplaces, improved environmental stewardship, enhanced operational resilience, and continual improvement, while reinforcing that the future success of AI in ESH depends as much on responsible governance and organizational culture as on technological advancement itself.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence may widen access to legal information while reproducing inequalities in who can use, evaluate and challenge its outputs. Research on gender and legal AI therefore needs to distinguish conditional willingness to use a service from confidence that its design supports trustworthy operation. This study examines that distinction in the supplied Group 10 Law-SDG database, linking gender and technology, procedural justice and digital inclusion perspectives. All 385 records inform descriptive analysis; comparisons between respondents recorded as female and male use 364 records, with the remaining gender responses retained descriptively. Item-level analysis combines distributional comparisons, stratified bootstrap intervals, paired contrasts and covariate-adjusted logistic models. Conditional willingness was endorsed by 307 records (79.7%), whereas 198 (51.4%) endorsed the proposition that inclusive design can improve trust. Their paired difference was 28.3 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval 21.8–34.8). The female-minus-male willingness difference was − 0.7 points (-9.0-7.5); the adjusted difference was 1.0 point (-7.4-9.4). Inclusive-design trust expectations and discrimination salience likewise showed small estimated gender contrasts with substantial uncertainty. Low block reliability precluded latent-scale modelling. The findings support neither a gender-deficit explanation nor a claim of established equality: similar reported willingness can coexist with unequal access and unmeasured exposure to harm. The contribution is a measurement-conscious distinction between conditional acceptance, trust expectations and substantive inclusion. Interpretation remains bounded by undocumented recruitment and by codebook labels identifying respondent sequences and comments as synthetic; numeric response provenance requires verification before these records can support claims about a human population.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) may change professional tasks, but the implications for workers depend on how technology is introduced and how people adapt. This study examines stated perceptions of task change, concern about routine work and AI-related learning in 385 adult, AI-aware questionnaire records from Bangladesh. Most respondents were recorded as law students, and the dataset does not establish that all participants were employed or young professionals. The questions do not directly measure current job security or the effects of AI exposure on employment. Individual items are therefore analysed separately using response distributions, paired endorsement comparisons and exploratory rank correlations. Of 385 respondents, 232 (60.3%) agreed that AI may reduce demand for some routine professional tasks; 307 (79.7%) agreed that learning to work effectively with AI could reduce their future job-security concerns; and 211 (54.8%) anticipated new tasks requiring human judgement and oversight. A total of 184 respondents endorsed both the routine-task concern and the potential reassurance of learning. These statements differ in meaning and do not establish whether training actually reduces insecurity. Exploratory correlations were small and should not be interpreted causally. Job demands-resources theory, psychological contract theory and career construction provide complementary lenses rather than validated models. The study distinguishes concern about tasks from concern about losing a job and identifies the need for independently verified employment status, recruitment documentation and direct measures of perceived job security in future research.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract This study examines how mainstream English-language newspapers evaluated entries in AI photography competitions compared to those in traditional photography competitions between 2015 and 2025. Drawing on Bourdieu’s field theory, symbolic capital and boundary construction, the study treats photography competitions as institutional fields where legitimacy is publicly negotiated and views newspapers as cultural intermediaries that translate these negotiations into broader public discourse. Employing a comparative longitudinal qualitative content analysis approach, the study analyzed three corpora constructed using Factiva, comprising traditional competitions, AI competitions, and AI rule controversies, to examine shifts in the evaluation criteria, tone, and timing of newspaper coverage. In traditional competition coverage, newspapers primarily evaluate entries based on established criteria such as technical quality, composition, impact, and social significance. However, in AI-related reporting, the focus shifts to the authorship, information disclosure, fairness, category relevance, authenticity, and public trust. The tone of the reports also varies across different corpora: traditional reports are mostly neutral or supportive, while those in the AI field tend to be more skeptical. Later, as the debate intensified, reports increasingly focused on procedural issues, emphasizing rule changes, disclosure requirements, and institutional oversight. Eventually, the evaluative paradigm shifted from photographic quality to boundary conflicts and formal governance.

Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into university learning, raising questions about dependency-oriented reliance and self-regulation. Drawing on a self-regulated learning perspective, this study examined associations among GenAI dependency, effort regulation, and multidimensional perceived learning outcomes, including the statistical indirect association involving effort regulation. Methods Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 982 students at three higher education institutions in Guangdong Province, China. Confirmatory factor analysis and covariance-based structural equation modeling were conducted, with indirect associations tested using 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for GenAI use frequency. Results The measurement model showed acceptable fit (CFI = 0.953, TLI = 0.944, RMSEA = 0.043, SRMR = 0.041). GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes ( β = −0.087) and was negatively associated with effort regulation ( β = −0.257). Effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes ( β = 0.497). The residual direct association was nonsignificant ( β = 0.041), whereas the indirect association was negative and significant ( β = −0.128). After adjustment for GenAI use frequency, the indirect association remained significant, but the small total association was no longer significant. Conclusion The findings highlight effort regulation as a relevant learner-controlled process in the association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. They also distinguish dependency-oriented reliance from frequency of GenAI use. The cross-sectional design and potential classroom clustering warrant cautious interpretation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools are widely reported to improve writing quality and efficiency, yet their implications for autonomy, defined here as volitional, informed, and self-endorsed decision-making, remain underexplored. Drawing on an integrated Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and Sociocultural Theory (SCT) framework, this study interviewed twenty second-language (L2) English learners in Hong Kong universities about how they perceive and report their interaction practices when using GenAI in L2 academic writing. Hybrid inductive/deductive thematic analysis of the interview data yielded six themes: selective and strategic deployment of GenAI; concerns about dependency; preservation of authorial voice; perceived benefits; critical evaluation of outputs; and awareness of institutional expectations. Learners described balancing efficiency against authentic authorship, editing or reframing AI-generated text to protect their voice, and treating GenAI as a peripheral rather than primary agent. From these reported practices we derived a heuristic of seven roles that learners ascribed to GenAI: text analyst, consultant, literature search/review instrument, tutor, creative aid, adversary, and conversational partner. Implications are drawn for pedagogy that treats GenAI as a mediational tool whose contributions must be subordinated to the writer’s own intellectual agenda.

This study examined generative artificial intelligence (AI) literacy, output verification and responsible use among undergraduate pre-service teachers at the University of Ilorin, Nigeria. The study adopted a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised 10,377 pre-service teachers, from which a sample size of 370 respondents was determined using the Krejcie and Morgan sample size table. Data were collected using a researcher-developed questionnaire titled Generative AI Literacy, Output Verification and Responsible Use Questionnaire (GAILORUQ). The instrument was validated by experts to ensure clarity, relevance and alignment with the study objectives. A pilot test involving 37 pre-service teachers outside the main study sample was conducted to establish the instrument’s internal consistency. Cronbach’s alpha yielded a reliability coefficient of 0.80. Data were analysed using mean and standard deviation to answer five research questions on generative AI literacy, output verification, responsible AI use, instructional applications and challenges encountered by pre-service teachers. The results indicated a moderate level of generative AI literacy, with a grand mean of 2.50, while output verification practices and awareness of responsible AI use were low, with grand means of 2.32 and 2.40, respectively. The extent of generative AI use for teaching and learning activities was high, with a grand mean of 3.15. The challenges encountered when applying generative AI to academic and instructional activities were also high, with a grand mean of 3.16. The findings established a gap between pre-service teachers’ use of generative AI tools and their practices for verifying AI-generated information and applying responsible AI principles. The study recommended that the University of Ilorin strengthen practical AI literacy training, promote systematic verification of AI-generated content, provide clear guidelines on responsible AI use, and integrate ethical generative AI practices into undergraduate teacher education programmes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can participate in literary composition by proposing plots, producing passages and revising prose. Its participation raises questions about the position from which a work is imagined, judged and presented to readers. This paper examines the reconstruction of literary subjectivity through theoretical argument and analysis of research on assisted writing. It distinguishes subjectivity from observable interaction, the institutional attribution of authorship and evaluations of textual quality. Literary theories of authorship and dialogue are brought into conversation with accounts of writing processes and technological mediation, with attention to their different explanatory purposes. A comparative framework considers intention, lived experience, narrative form and responsibility across conception, drafting and revision. The analysis identifies tensions involving delegated intention, narrative anchoring, simulated experience, stylistic specificity and public attribution. It proposes that agency can be sustained through active reconsideration of creative aims, consequential aesthetic judgement, attention to experiential and cultural particularity, and accountable relations with readers. These are analytical proposals, not a validated measure of subjectivity. Existing studies concern specific interfaces and writing tasks and cannot establish a universal effect on literary identity. The paper reports no new experiment or interviews; its focus is short fiction and novel writing.

Precision oncology requires accurate molecular insights, yet obtaining these directly from genomics is costly and time-consuming for broad clinical use. Predicting complex molecular features and patient prognosis directly from routine whole-slide images (WSI) remains a major challenge for current deep learning methods. Here we introduce PathLUPI, which uses transcriptomic privileged information during training to extract genome-anchored histological embeddings, enabling effective molecular prediction using only WSIs at inference. Through extensive evaluation across 49 molecular oncology tasks using 11,257 cases among 20 cohorts, PathLUPI demonstrated superior performance compared to conventional methods trained solely on WSIs. Crucially, it achieves AUC $\geq$ 0.80 in 14 of the biomarker prediction and molecular subtyping tasks and C-index $\geq$ 0.70 in survival cohorts of 5 major cancer types. Moreover, PathLUPI embeddings reveal distinct cellular morphological signatures associated with specific genotypes and related biological pathways within WSIs. By effectively encoding molecular context to refine WSI representations, PathLUPI overcomes a key limitation of existing models and offers a novel strategy to bridge molecular insights with routine pathology workflows for wider clinical application.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: The burgeoning intensity and frequency of both natural and human-made disasters are posing substantial challenges to all facets of societies worldwide, requiring accurate, timely, and data-driven decision-making systems for efficient emergency response and disaster management. The implications of different geospatial technological advancements, such as remote sensing, Geographic Information Systems, and Global Navigation Satellite Systems, are emerging as vital analytical tools for improving the components of the disaster management cycle. This chapter focuses on applications of geospatial technologies toward strengthening the framework of the disaster management system by offering real-time situational awareness, coordinated emergency operations and risk assessment. It includes the examination of the inclusion of geospatial databases, unmanned aerial vehicles, and satellite imagery for damage assessment, vulnerability analysis, and hazard mapping for natural disasters. The importance of geospatial applications in evacuation planning, early warning systems, allocation of resources, and post-disaster recovery planning is also highlighted. With fast-paced technological advancements such as big data analytics, digital twins, and smart sensor IoT systems, geospatial technologies are also being utilized in emergency response through damage assessment, search and rescue operations, logistics planning, and real-time situational awareness systems. Barriers and challenges related to accuracy, scalability, and availability of data are critically assessed, and a brief discussion highlighting future opportunities and best practices is presented for improving the effectiveness of strategies related to disaster management and emergency response in alignment with the Sustainable Development Goals.

Collaborative cross-cultural learning expands higher education students’ (HES’) intercultural and language awareness, enhances their intercultural competence, has an impact on attitudes towards technology and AI as well as towards the course design and general satisfaction with the collaborative experience in the course. Furthermore, their self-perceived role in a digital setting and their self-perceived English proficiency were measured. The CoGIH Project encourages HES to explore the educational potential of artificial intelligence (AI) for learning and teaching in the school setting. A special focus is on the impact AI might have on the language learning process in English as a lingua franca in a multilingual setting. N = 113 HES, including both pre-service and in-service teachers as well as students preparing for educational administration, from five institutions in Israel, Germany, and Hungary collaborated in 14 international groups, representing five higher education institutions; n = 91 answered the questionnaires. Each group investigated the educational potential of a specific AI application and developed an AI-supported, results-based webpage. The study employed a multi-method research design. Questionnaires were administered to the HES to investigate their experiences at the beginning and at the end of the course. While quantitative data were used to investigate the research through the lens of descriptive statistics and correlations between factors, qualitative data from the open questions were analysed to enable a deeper understanding of HES’ perceptions, experiences and meanings, as well as their critical thinking. The study highlighted strengths and challenges in using AI for educational purposes. The HES valued clear structures, logical navigation, and creative, motivating tasks. Simultaneously, recurring issues included incomplete translations, limited depth of critical reflection, and weaknesses in visual design. In sum, even though AI can support creativity and language learning and teaching, individual learners’ reflections and authentic teacher guidance remain indispensable for meaningful learning.

Background: AI adoption in hospital administration raises governance questions about accountability, data security and oversight. Military hospitals add confidentiality and operational-continuity constraints. Guidance specific to military hospital administration is sparse. Objective: To propose a six-dimension governance framework for AI in military hospital administration, anchored in international guidance and a rapid scan of recent literature. Methods: Conceptual framework development. Principles were extracted from WHO, NIST and OECD instruments and mapped to hospital-administration functions. A rapid PubMed scan (three queries, 1 November 2026; 42 unique records reviewed at title/abstract level) tested whether published work addresses the topic. Results: Of 42 records, 13 concerned AI in military health care; one commentary on mental-health AI explicitly addressed governance. No reviewed record addressed AI governance in military hospital administration. A general cybersecurity scoping review found no machine-learning studies mapped to the NIST “Govern” function. The framework comprises six dimensions, a five-phase roadmap and ten candidate indicators. Conclusions: The scan suggests a literature gap . The framework is a conceptual proposal and has not been empirically validated; Delphi consultation and case studies are the logical next steps.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract When organizations delegate work to artificial intelligence (AI), controls that remain formally in place may no longer achieve their purposes. We combine systematic identification and selection with integrative analysis of 171 papers across five research streams and 26 supplementary sources. The synthesis develops dynamic control fit: an arrangement's ability to achieve a specified control function while sustaining or restoring the conditions on which that function depends. We explain this ability through a framework of three interconnected requirements: Deliver, Renew and Adapt. Deliver concerns whether coverage, information, expertise and opportunities to intervene support effective control in current work. Renew concerns the practice, feedback and maintenance through which these capabilities persist. Adapt concerns recognizing deficiencies, obtaining authorized changes and verifying restored performance. The framework explains how AI may improve immediate enforcement while reducing experiences through which people develop judgment for future oversight, although other activities may compensate. Coverage, reviewer capacity and revision authority impose distinct constraints requiring different responses. Continued reliance must also be assessed separately from performance because beliefs, external expectations and practical constraints can sustain or limit use. By following a specified function across changes in control arrangements, the review develops testable explanations of improvement, erosion, compensation and recovery.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Telehealth is increasingly supported by connected devices, remote monitoring, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and distributed computing. These tools can extend access and support more responsive care, but their computational and environmental demands are rarely considered alongside clinical and organizational needs. We describe the current Canadian telehealth landscape, including remote care management, virtual visits, patient portals, and remote monitoring, and identify opportunities and gaps for AI integration. We then define Green AI in healthcare and explain how an IoT-fog-cloud architecture can support resource-aware telehealth. For health leaders, Green AI is not only an engineering issue. It affects procurement, infrastructure planning, workforce capacity, clinical workflow, environmental responsibility, and equity. Evaluation should consider clinical performance, resource use, organizational fit, and sustainability. Responsible AI-enabled telehealth requires more than technical performance. A Green AI perspective can help health organizations improve computational efficiency while maintaining patient safety, usable workflows, resilience, and equitable access.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Smart materials, a transformative class of stimuli-responsive materials, are capable of responding to surrounding changes such as temperature, pressure, light, electric/magnetic fields, and chemical environments. Owing to their multifunctionality such as self-healing, self-cleaning, and self-triggering, smart materials are the potential candidates for diverse applications that include but are not limited to aerospace, healthcare, robotics, and energy systems. With the advent of new synthesis routes and fabrication methods, the progress in the field of smart material emerged with large and complex datasets, thus making this increasingly challenging to optimize the synthesis parameters and materials properties. The prediction of multifunctional behavior of smart materials using conventional experimental techniques (that requires trial-and-error runs) is eventually tedious, time consuming, and costly. Thanks to artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms. The AI–ML algorithms and predictive models have significantly transformed the field of smart materials in the sense that it can help in optimization in synthesis parameters, expedite the fabrication process, and property prediction, thereby enabling the development of multifunctional smart materials devices. Although there are ample numbers of research papers that highlight the AI-driven materials discovery of smart material, the comprehensive constructive reviews that further shed light on shortcomings of these studies are fewer in numbers. In view of this, the present chapter explores the AI-driven paradigm shift in smart materials, highlighting synthesis, fabrication, characterization, and property prediction. The first part of the chapter delves into AI-assisted parameters optimization in synthesis and fabrication of smart materials followed by integration of computational models with experimental data for fabricating the prototypes of multifunctional smart materials. Following this, the use of various AI techniques such as deep learning (DL), reinforcement learning, and generative models is discussed for materials discovery ranging from shape-memory alloys (SMAs) and piezoelectric composites to self-healing polymers. The predictive capability of Al–ML models for property prediction of smart materials is discussed in the midst for the chapter, while significant challenges that include but are not limited to data security, model reliability, and need for standard datasets are highlighted toward the end of the chapter followed by pathways to overcome these challenges. The future trajectory of AI–ML-driven innovations in smart materials in context of their potential to emerge as efficient and sustainable solution for next-generation materials is summarized in the last section.

Seeking health information is a common practice that helps individuals understand health conditions and manage illnesses. Among young people, this behaviour has increased due to the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, improved mobile phone capabilities, and widespread internet access. However, despite the speed and convenience AI applications provide, there is a risk of inaccurate or misleading information, especially when users’ health conditions differ from the data on which the AI systems were trained. This study assessed the use of AI applications on mobile phones for health information-seeking among university undergraduates in Anambra State. The main objective was to examine undergraduates’ health information-seeking behaviour in relation to their utilization of AI mobile applications. The study was anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Diffusion of Innovation theory. A quantitative survey design was adopted, using a structured Likert-scale questionnaire for data collection. From a population of 60,903 students, a sample size of 358 was determined using the Krejcie and Morgan formula. Data were analysed using mean scores, with 3.0 as the decision benchmark: items with mean scores below 3.0 were rejected, while those above 3.0 were accepted. Findings indicated that most respondents use AI applications on their mobile phones to seek health information, largely due to accessibility, convenience, and ease of interaction. The study concludes that although AI health information tools are useful, there is a need for greater caution and guidance regarding the quality of information accessed. It recommends the development and enforcement of stricter regulations on AI health information tools and the implementation of institutional educational programmes to improve students’ understanding of responsible AI use.

Migrant female workers in Bangladesh's ready-made garment (RMG) industry experience a disproportionate burden of occupational, reproductive, mental, and infectious health problems, compounded by limited access to quality healthcare services. This study proposes a Health Needs Assessment (HNA) protocol to systematically identify priority health needs, assess existing healthcare services, and develop evidence-informed interventions to improve worker health and well-being. The protocol employs the five-step Cavanagh and Chadwick Health Needs Assessment model and adopts a mixed-methods approach, incorporating surveys, questionnaires, focus group discussions, key informant interviews, and health data analysis. Public participation and stakeholder engagement are integrated throughout the assessment to ensure context-specific and feasible recommendations. The protocol is designed to identify healthcare gaps, prioritize health concerns, and inform sustainable workplace health strategies. This framework provides a structured, evidence-based approach for strengthening occupational health services and supporting policy development for migrant female garment workers in Bangladesh. Medicine Today 2026, Vol.38 (2): 180-184
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Digital platforms have diversified the ways in which health professionals engage with patients and created additional opportunities for members of the public to solicit help from those with professional expertise. Consequently, we find online spaces in which trained health professionals are available to respond to queries and to administer health advice. What differentiates such spaces from other kinds of web-based interactions is the centrality of the health professional and the foregrounding of professional medical expertise. More recently, artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as chatbots have been utilised to administer such expertise, extending the availability of information purportedly legitimated by the input of medical experts. In this chapter, we consider how users submitting health queries articulate what is of concern to them and how both human and automated responders construct an expert persona.

Abstract HealthSync AI (HSAI) is an intelligent health monitoring system designed to make personal healthcare more accessible, convenient, and proactive through the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and software technology. In today's busy lifestyle, people may overlook changes in their health until they become serious, highlighting the need for continuous monitoring and timely awareness. HealthSync AI addresses this need by providing a desktop application where users can manage their health profiles, monitor vital signs and physical activity through compatible Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) devices, and store their health information securely in a user-specific database. The system uses AI-based analysis to examine available health readings, identify unusual patterns, and provide personalized health insights and general wellness recommendations. It also incorporates features such as nearby hospital discovery, emergency contact support, and outbreak-related information to help users make more informed decisions. By combining wearable sensor data, intelligent analysis, and an easy-to-use interface, HealthSync AI aims to encourage healthier habits and support early awareness of potential health concerns. The system is intended to complement, rather than replace, professional medical advice and diagnosis. Right now, our healthcare system is fundamentally reactive, meaning people usually only end up in a hospital after their symptoms have already become severe. Most healthcare apps available today are pretty limited, functioning mostly as digital filing cabinets for storing medical records or simple tools for booking appointments. On a broader scale, public health authorities are constantly fighting an uphill battle. Because medical data is scattered across different systems and reporting is often delayed, officials struggle to spot disease outbreaks at an early stage when intervention could actually save lives. To move far beyond the single-metric limitations of typical open-source projects, HealthSync AI is designed to ingest and process eleven distinct telemetry streams simultaneously, offering a complete and continuous window into a user's physiological state. This multi-parameter data doesn't just sit in a silo; it is securely managed through local SQLite persistence and channeled into an intelligent backend framework that processes structured health observations rather than relying on superficial, generic API wrapper chatbots. The platform also tackles the broader systemic issues of delayed reporting and fragmented medical data by introducing integrated outbreak analysis. While traditional systems leave public health authorities struggling to spot community-level risks in time, HealthSync AI bridges individual continuous monitoring with aggregated insights to help track potential health threats at an early stage. Combined with built-in emergency response features and a clean separation of responsibilities across its BLE, database, and UI layers, HealthSync AI transforms personal wellness tracking and community health intelligence into a single, cohesive, and future-ready solution.

Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) has rapidly entered clinical environments, posing a risk of "cognitive offloading" that may impede the development of independent clinical judgment. This study conducted a cross-sectional survey of residents, fellows, and faculty at a large academic medical center in January 2026 to quantify Gen-AI utilization and perceptions in physical medicine and rehabilitation (PM&R) to inform curriculum development. Thirty-six trainees (95% response rate) and 11 faculty members (30% response rate) completed the survey; 43 (91.5%) reported any Gen-AI use and formed the analytic sample. Among users, 72.1% used Gen-AI daily for clinical learning and 51.2% during patient encounters, yet 67.4% were self-taught and only 7.0% always requested citations. Trainees requested citations more often than faculty (P=.048), while faculty more often relied on clinical judgment without additional verification (62.5% vs. 25.7%, P=.089). Gen-AI-derived evidence was rarely surfaced in teaching: 60.5% discussed it during case presentations rarely or never, and only 16.2% always disclosed its origin. Residents are integrating Gen-AI into clinical workflows at rates that outpace faculty familiarity, while verification remains largely undiscussed and untaught. These gaps highlight an urgent need for structured Gen-AI curricula in PM&R residency.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This research compares interaction structures in comments posted on TikTok, a platform whose content visibility and dissemination are algorithmically mediated, and derives theoretical and design implications for generative artificial intelligence. Using the Community of Inquiry (CoI) model, the study compares the configuration of social, cognitive, and teaching presence in interactions generated by Ibero-American edutokers with varying levels of visibility. A cross-sectional comparative design is employed, contrasting three different videos (and their associated comment threads) per creator, utilizing deductive coding and relational network analysis. The results show that comments on creators’ first videos are dominated by socially oriented participation (open communication, group cohesion, and emotional expression), whereas cognitive-presence categories are comparatively more prevalent in comments on creators’ most recent videos. Comments on the most-viewed videos form larger and more dispersed networks of associations, in which cognitive categories co-occur less cohesively than in comments on the most recent videos. The most cohesive co-occurrence patterns link exploration, integration, and resolution, rather than reflecting the volume of participation. The findings suggest design considerations for AI-assisted learning environments in which generative AI may amplify interaction while requiring pedagogical mechanisms that preserve conceptual continuity. As a cross-sectional comparison of different videos rather than a repeated-measures panel of the same commenters, these patterns should be read as associative rather than developmental, and generative AI systems were not examined directly in this study.

This study examines whether adopting artificial intelligence tools is associated with entrepreneurial success among women entrepreneurs in Tunisia, which business capabilities carry that association, and under what conditions it is stronger. The study uses a cross-sectional survey of 350 women who own, jointly own or principally manage a business that uses at least one AI tool. Respondents were recruited through women’s business associations, incubators and entrepreneurial networks, with quotas by region and sector. The data were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling. Four capabilities (operational efficiency, market and customer capability, innovation capacity, and financial readiness) are tested as mediators. Digital skills and institutional support are tested as moderators. AI adoption has a positive direct association with entrepreneurial success (β = 0.200, p < .001). The four specific indirect effects are all positive and sum to 0.330, giving a total effect of 0.530 at mean moderator levels and indicating complementary partial mediation. Market and customer capability is the largest pathway (0.120). Digital skills (interaction β = 0.120, p = .003) and institutional support (interaction β = 0.100, p = .004) both strengthen the direct association. The model explains 62.0% of the variance in entrepreneurial success. Entrepreneurs should start with clearly defined tasks, especially marketing and customer service, and pair adoption with hands-on training. Support organisations can combine tool access with mentoring, practical skills programmes and guidance on responsible data use. The study offers gender-focused evidence on AI and business outcomes in Tunisia, a setting where earlier SME studies do not report results by owner gender. The findings are associations within a sample of AI users and need longitudinal testing before causal claims are made.

Generative AI (GenAI) has rapidly moved from novelty to ubiquity, reshaping how doctoral students approach learning, research, and career preparation. Yet while universities and the public often frame debates around undergraduate use, comparatively little attention has been given to PhD students despite their dual role as learners and future scholars. In this paper, we reflect on our experiences as PhD students using GenAI across coursework, qualifying exams, thesis research, teaching, and the job market. Drawing on these experiences, we highlight both the opportunities GenAI provides—for efficiency, conceptual clarity, and skill development—and the ethical challenges it raises, including concerns about academic integrity, cognitive outsourcing, disclosure, and employability beyond academia. Our reflections emphasize that GenAI use is not uniform: it varies with disciplinary context, institutional policies, and students’ levels of development. We argue that GenAI is no longer peripheral to doctoral education but central to its practice, and the challenge ahead is how it can be integrated responsibly to support learning, uphold integrity, and prepare graduates for an evolving academic and professional landscape.

Purpose This study aims to examine how innovative work behavior (IWB) influences hospital performance (HP), with professional characteristics (ProC) and patient characteristics (PtC) as mediating factors. Furthermore, it examines whether the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) moderates this relationship. Design/methodology/approach A structured questionnaire was used to collect data from 351 healthcare professionals in Pakistan. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was applied to test the hypotheses. Findings The results reveal that IWB has a significant, positive effect on HP, both directly and indirectly through ProC and PtC. These characteristics act as important underlying mechanisms through which IWB enhances performance outcomes. While AI adoption does not directly improve HP, it positively moderates the IWB–HP relationship, indicating that AI strengthens the performance outcomes of innovation-supportive environments. Originality/value This study integrates the resource-based view and job demands–resources into a nomological framework. It contributes to healthcare innovation research by showing that technological adoption alone is insufficient; employee innovative behavior and human-related characteristics are crucial drivers of HP.

ABSTRACT The use of generative artificial intelligence in education creates opportunities for students to access information and understand learning materials more flexibly. However, such accessibility does not necessarily correspond to students’ ability to manage their own learning independently, particularly in Islamic Religious Education (PAI) at the junior secondary school level. This study aims to examine the relationship between the use of ChatGPT as a learning resource and students’ learning independence at SMPN 5 Ambarawa. A quantitative approach with a correlational design was employed, involving 64 students selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using a four-point Likert-scale questionnaire measuring ChatGPT utilization and learning independence. The data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 27 through descriptive statistics, instrument validity and reliability testing, and Spearman’s rho correlation analysis. The results revealed a positive and statistically significant relationship between ChatGPT utilization and students’ learning independence, with a correlation coefficient of 0.598 and a significance value of p < 0.001. These findings indicate that better utilization of ChatGPT tends to be associated with higher levels of learning independence. Nevertheless, this relationship does not establish a causal effect. The use of ChatGPT in Islamic Religious Education should therefore be accompanied by teacher guidance, information verification, and active student engagement to ensure that the technology is used critically and responsibly. ABSTRAK Pemanfaatan kecerdasan buatan generatif dalam pembelajaran membuka peluang bagi siswa untuk memperoleh informasi dan memahami materi secara lebih fleksibel. Namun, kemudahan akses tersebut belum tentu sejalan dengan kemampuan siswa mengelola proses belajarnya secara mandiri, khususnya dalam mata pelajaran Pendidikan Agama Islam (PAI) di jenjang sekolah menengah pertama. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis hubungan antara pemanfaatan ChatGPT sebagai sumber belajar dan kemandirian belajar siswa di SMPN 5 Ambarawa. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan desain korelasional yang melibatkan 64 siswa melalui teknik purposive sampling. Data dikumpulkan menggunakan angket skala Likert empat pilihan yang mengukur pemanfaatan ChatGPT dan kemandirian belajar. Data dianalisis menggunakan IBM SPSS Statistics versi 27 melalui statistik deskriptif, pengujian validitas dan reliabilitas instrumen, serta korelasi Spearman’s rho. Hasil analisis menunjukkan hubungan positif dan signifikan antara pemanfaatan ChatGPT dan kemandirian belajar siswa, dengan koefisien korelasi sebesar 0,598 dan nilai signifikansi p < 0,001. Temuan ini menunjukkan bahwa pemanfaatan ChatGPT yang lebih baik cenderung berkaitan dengan kemandirian belajar yang lebih tinggi. Meskipun demikian, hubungan tersebut tidak membuktikan sebab-akibat. Penggunaan ChatGPT dalam pembelajaran PAI perlu disertai bimbingan guru, verifikasi informasi, dan keterlibatan aktif siswa agar teknologi dimanfaatkan secara kritis dan bertanggung jawab.

Chronic ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure is associated with several ocular disorders, particularly cataract and pterygium. Previous studies have largely focused on rural populations such as farmers and fishermen, while evidence among urban outdoor workers remains limited. This study examined the association between worker characteristics and ocular disorders among Public Infrastructure and Facilities Maintenance Officers (Petugas Penanganan Prasarana dan Sarana Umum [PPSU]) in Jakarta, Indonesia. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 53 PPSU workers in South Jakarta. Data included age, sex, duration of employment, and ocular examination findings. Cataract and pterygium were identified through direct eye examinations. Descriptive statistics summarized participant characteristics and ocular disorder prevalence. Associations between independent variables and cataract were assessed using Fisher’s Exact Test and Prevalence Ratios (PR). Robust Poisson regression was used to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios (aPR). Cataract was detected in 22.6% of participants, despite a mean age of 38.77 years. Workers aged ≥40 years had a substantially higher cataract prevalence than those aged <40 years (PR=12.32; 95% CI: 1.71–88.77). After adjustment for employment duration, age remained independently associated with cataract (aPR=3.14; 95% CI: 1.48–6.67; p=0.003). Employment duration was not significantly associated with cataract after adjustment (aPR=1.51; 95% CI: 0.46–4.96; p=0.496). No significant associations were observed for pterygium. Ocular disorders were common among urban outdoor workers. Older age was independently associated with cataract. These findings support regular eye screening, UV protection, and preventive occupational health programs for outdoor workers in tropical settings.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has become a groundbreaking initiative that transforms the essence of the functioning of Human Resource Management (HRM), its capabilities, and its strategic value. With organizations working in information-driven and technology-driven settings, AI technologies are being incorporated into recruitment, selection, performance management, learning and development, and employee engagement systems. The paper analyzes the role of AI in HRM that is currently changing by summarizing the current literature and providing empirical evidence of a mixed method research on HR practitioners in various sectors. The findings reveal that AI is able to help optimize decision-making, improve operational efficiency, predictive capabilities, and workforce analytics and that it also has issues that concern the ethical utilization, data privacy, and the possibility of algorithmic bias. The results support the idea that the value of AI should not be in offering an alternative to human resource professionals but rather enhance them with making evidence-based and strategic decisions. The paper ends with the organizational implication on those organizations interested in adopting AI in a responsible manner, and future HR technology research.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: In the context of the urban digital revolution, recruitment through AI technologies has become common practice to address competition in the labor market. However, it is still unclear how the effectiveness of such recruitment is connected with humanistic values. For this research, an exploratory qualitative research design was used, involving semi-structured interviews with eight human resource professionals in Shanghai. Based on the results, the use of AI in recruitment led to increased efficiency mainly when screening candidates through high-volume, standardized processes, although the promised efficiency was not delivered in practice because the introduction of the AI system increased the workload. Patterns of human-machine cooperation were observed in different companies: tech companies and foreign companies are inclined to adopt interactive adjustment approaches, while state-owned enterprises retain human-dominated decision-making. Transparency of algorithms was still lacking in numerous instances, and there was an asymmetry in the accountability framework of algorithms, wherein disobeying algorithms carries more personal consequences than obeying them. The more experienced professionals became more autonomous in their work, while the less experienced professionals depended more on the algorithm. Issues like management support, information accuracy, and departmental integration have a major impact on implementation. This study contributes to the theory of human-machine collaboration by proposing the concept of asymmetric algorithmic accountability, which captures the uneven distribution of organizational consequences for following versus overriding AI recommendations and shapes practitioner behavior in ways that extend beyond individual trust or algorithmic transparency.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The present schooling system is currently facing a dual disruptive crisis, spurred by the encroachment of social media algorithms and generative Artificial Intelligence (AI). While these forces impact the way students learn and think about information, they also induce an epistemological overhaul in the ecology of instructional communication. Students, with their visual rhetorical frameworks from digital platforms and the use of AI for analytical processing, present an apparent disciplinary crisis for their educators-a communication crisis in disguise. Applying Karl Weick's Sensemaking theory, this paper examines school leaders and Guidance Counselors in Samarinda, Indonesia's understanding of these ambiguities and reconceptualization of their roles. Through qualitative case studies based on teachers' pedagogical narratives, this study shows that teachers' epistemological authority is diminishing as they negotiate the hegemonic algorithmic communication. They respond to the students' fear of cognitive degradation by reorienting from a "knowledge transmitting" communicative practice towards "ethical verifiers" and "empathetic listeners." A Human-AI symbiosis is being created with the machine as information provider and humans as ethical validators and empathic listener. Implications were made for the development of policies related to algorithmic communication literacy and the application of tactical empathy in the classroom.

Abstract High-dimensional cellular phenotypes can motivate biological hypotheses, but similarity alone cannot establish mechanism or causal validity. DISCOVERY-AGENT links exploratory JUMP Cell Painting evidence with evidence-grounded hypothesis generation, independent critique and bounded human-review routing. An initial 65-record CRISPR/ORF analysis across nine gene–modality tests found four FDR-significant CRISPR plate-level associations (AKT1, BRCA1, MTOR and TP53), none among evaluated ORF genes. A distinct later cross-source compound-identity benchmark used 614 morphological features and achieved AUROC 0.6142 on 1,250 held-out compounds with training-only preprocessing; this is identity discrimination, not mechanism-of-action classification. Three structured hypotheses underwent LLM critique and revision, while eleven gene-pair evidence assessments yielded no FDR-significant mechanistic finding (minimum q = 0.2037). Archived governance checks passed 1,021/1,021 predefined tests; nevertheless, the initial live-agent run contained two execution errors among five cases, with both cases responding on fresh retest. These findings demonstrate feasibility of auditable evidence processing and modest cross-source morphology signal, not validated autonomous discovery, prospective safety, or completed expert review. The work delineates practical requirements for independent biological validation and reproducible scientific agents.

This paper explores the transformative integration of Hybrid Intelligence (HI) within the landscape of higher philological education, specifically operationalized through the innovative 'Literary Detective' pedagogical framework. Amidst the shifting cognitive baselines of the digital era, this study addresses the crisis of sustained deep attention by proposing a synergistic model of textual archaeology. The research focuses on the intricate process of multidimensional decoding, wherein human cultural intuition collaborates with the computational power of Large Language Models (LLMs) to excavate latent intertextual layers across a diverse literary corpus.The study provides a comparative analysis of foundational and modern texts, demonstrating how a structured Decoding Matrix facilitates the identification of complex cultural codes in the cosmological epics of Vaja-Pshavela, the impressionistic prose of Niko Lortkipanidze, and the tragic war poetry of Mirza Gelovani, alongside the works of Homer, Margaret Atwood, and Ana Kalandadze. The findings reveal that Artificial Intelligence, when utilized as a cognitive scaffold rather than a replacement for authorial voice, significantly amplifies the student's capacity to navigate intertextual networks and resolve “artificial hallucinations” through intuitive filtering. Empirical evidence suggests that this hybrid approach not only increases the efficiency of thematic identification by approximately 38% but also fosters advanced critical thinking and digital literacy. Ultimately, the paper argues for a paradigm shift in the humanities, positioning the student as an active investigator in an AI-augmented hermeneutic environment, ensuring the continued relevance of philological rigor in a post-digital academic world.
topics: Interdisciplinary Studies: Technology, Society, and Humanities

documents.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) offers substantial societal benefits, but it also can pose significant hazards to workers. Methods A scoping literature review was conducted to identify materials published from 2010 to 2025 and indicative of artificial intelligence (AI) hazards to workers. The aim was to answer two research questions: What are the potential occupational safety and health hazards associated with exposure to AI? and What are the approaches that have been proposed to control these hazards in the workplace? Results Eight databases and grey literature were searched. These yielded 25,925 studies, which after screening resulted in 622 studies for full text review. Of these, 216 were eligible for data extraction. These studies substantiated 14 categories of potential hazards to workers from AI. These categories included: threats of physical trauma; dehumanization of workers; threats to human agency, autonomy, and workers’ voice; loss of human and workplace connection; threats to sense of self and identity; threats of increased stress, fatigue, and work-life imbalance from work intensification; dependence on AI, leading to deterioration of skills; potential exacerbation of OSH inequities in the workplace; threats of weakening the psychological contract, worker engagement, and trust; threats of job loss, unemployment, disruption of labor market, and reduced economic mobility; threats of underpaid, precarious, and hidden work; threats of cyberphysical attacks and bullying; inappropriate worker monitoring, surveillance, management, and selection; and threats of adverse consequences of worker cognitive and physical augmentation and enhancement. Control approaches also were identified for each hazard category. Discussion This study provides a comprehensive appraisal of AI-related potential OSH hazards and controls and offers a foundation for future research and practice.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Traditional fishermen who catch green mussels face various potential occupational hazards; however, systematic identification of Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) hazards has never been conducted in the Kamal Muara area, North Jakarta. This study aimed to identify OHS hazards using the Hazard Identification approach (the identification stage within the HIRA framework) in green mussel catching activities among traditional fishermen in Kamal Muara in 2026. This was a descriptive study using a qualitative analytical approach. Data were collected through structured observations and in-depth interviews with nine informants selected using purposive sampling, consisting of key informants, main informants, and supporting informants. Data were analyzed through data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing, with validation conducted through source triangulation and method triangulation. The results showed 24 potential hazards across all work stages, namely preparation, travel, diving, returning, and unloading, which were classified into eight hazard categories: physical, chemical, biological, ergonomic, psychosocial, mechanical, environmental, and physiological hazards. The diving stage had the highest number and greatest variety of hazards, including the potential for compressor failure during diving, leaking or kinked air hoses, and the absence of a compressor operator on the boat, making this stage the main priority for OHS attention. It is recommended that equipment inspections be conducted before going to sea, appropriate personal protective equipment be used, weather conditions be monitored, and OHS training be provided for traditional fishermen.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The overall rapid increase in the use of artificial intelligence technologies (AIT) is linked to various initiatives that propose AI ‘for good’. However, a holistic, in-depth understanding of these AI use cases and their implications for people, society, and the planet remains lacking, beyond the respective projects’ self-descriptions. To close this gap, we present a framework for a holistic yet manageable approach for running AI projects to assess their impact. We call our approach the Impact AI Method, as we not only want to assess the impacts of AI use cases but also want to impact AI and its use in practice and in public debate. The Impact AI Method evaluates concrete AI use cases in terms of their contribution to sustainability and public interest, reflecting these two concepts as well as established international guiding principles such as democratic values and human rights. The interview- and survey-based methodological approach combines and extends existing assessment approaches, incorporating a catalogue of 25 assessment criteria to evaluate the results. The Impact AI Method is intended as a reusable blueprint to inform public debate about AI ‘for good’ claims and to support the creation of evidence and transparency for AI systems that purport to contribute to just and sustainable development.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: With the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence, new possibilities have emerged for addressing problems in project-based learning at the compulsory education stage, such as insufficient teacher guidance resources and inadequate personalized support for students. Based on literature research, this paper analyzes the implementation challenges faced by artificial intelligence-empowered project-based learning from the dual perspectives of teachers and students. The study finds that, at the teacher level, there are three types of problems: superficial AI application, generalized technology embedding, and fragmented instructional design. At the student level, there are difficulties such as the substitution of the inquiry process, interference with learning engagement, and compression of the space for collaborative construction. In response to these problems, this paper proposes optimization strategies, including promoting subject-differentiated technical support, designing structured collaborative learning sheets, improving the formative evaluation system, and enhancing teachers’ AI literacy, with a view to providing references for the deep integration of artificial intelligence and project-based learning in compulsory education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative video technology presents novel opportunities for visual effects (VFX) asset generation, yet full reliance on artificial intelligence often creates visual inconsistencies, reduced artistic control, and integration barriers with live-action footage. This article aims to analyze the integration of generative video into the VFX post-production workflow of the short film “SPLIT//SECOND” and evaluate its effectiveness relative to conventional computer-generated imagery (CGI) practices. Employing a practice-based research methodology, the production applied a hybrid workflow where live-action footage serves as the physical reality anchor while artificial intelligence assets construct surreal virtual reality (VR) elements. Empirical results demonstrate that generative video substantially accelerates visual asset acquisition with up to 95% time efficiency, reducing manual tasks from 60–90 minutes to approximately 30 seconds to 3 minutes. Although it eliminates manual modeling labor, this method does not remove the essential requirements of digital compositing, rotoscoping, tracking, and color matching, while also introducing variable operating costs driven by platform credit consumption. ABSTRAK Perkembangan teknologi generative video membuka peluang baru dalam penyediaan aset visual effects (VFX), namun penggunaannya secara mandiri kerap memicu kendala konsistensi visual, penurunan kontrol artistik, dan hambatan integrasi dengan rekaman live-action. Artikel ini bertujuan menganalisis integrasi generative video dalam workflow produksi VFX pada film pendek “SPLIT//SECOND” serta membandingkan efektivitasnya dengan pendekatan computer-generated imagery (CGI) konvensional. Penciptaan karya menerapkan metode practice-based research melalui hybrid workflow yang menempatkan rekaman live-action sebagai jangkar realitas fisik dan elemen berbasis kecerdasan buatan (artificial intelligence / AI) sebagai pembangun dunia virtual reality (VR). Pengujian empiris membuktikan bahwa pemanfaatan generative video mampu mempercepat penyediaan aset visual secara signifikan dengan efisiensi waktu mencapai 95%, yakni dari durasi manual sekitar 60–90 menit menjadi hanya 30 detik hingga 3 menit. Kendati memangkas tahapan teknis permodelan manual, pendekatan ini tidak mengeliminasi kebutuhan digital compositing, rotoscoping, tracking, dan color matching, serta menimbulkan konsekuensi beban biaya variabel berbasis konsumsi credits.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing drug discovery through data-driven and generative methods throughout the pharmaceutical pipeline. The literature review points to the recent developments in AI-driven target discovery, compound screening, de novo molecular design, ADMET prediction, and protein structure modeling. It describes how traditional machine-learning models have been replaced with contemporary generative and multimodel models that combine molecular and omics data. Popular tools and benches like DeepChem, RDKit, or MoleculeNet also are mentioned. Although the speed at which drugs are developed is on the rise, as well as the cost, there are still difficulties with data quality, interpretability, and regulatory acceptance. Future directions include physics-informed modeling and explainable AI, which would be helpful in reliable and clinically relevant drug discovery.

This chapter presents a practical framework for integrating AI into ESH Management Systems through the authors’ strategic framework of P olicy and Commitment, R isk Management, I mplementation and Operations, and M onitoring and Continuous Improvement (PRIM). Building upon the AI life cycle introduced in the previous chapter, PRIM provides a structured governance approach that enables organizations to responsibly deploy, operate, and continually improve AI applications within existing ESH management processes. This chapter demonstrates how PRIM aligns with established continuous improvement models, including PDCA, allowing organizations to integrate AI while maintaining regulatory compliance, ethical decision-making, and organizational accountability. It examines key considerations for AI policy development, algorithmic bias assessment, data quality, model validation, operational readiness, cybersecurity, human oversight, performance metrics, and continual improvement. This chapter also explores opportunities for AI-enabled automation, predictive analytics, and enhanced decision-making through technologies such as smart sensors, computer vision, wearable devices, and real-time data analytics. Practical examples illustrate how AI can improve hazard identification, exposure monitoring, equipment reliability, regulatory compliance, and workplace safety by shifting ESH Management from reactive reporting to proactive risk prevention. Finally, this chapter discusses the technical, operational, ethical, regulatory, organizational, and cultural limitations associated with AI implementation, emphasizing that successful integration depends upon disciplined governance, continuous monitoring, and informed human judgment. Together, the concepts presented establish PRIM as a practical methodology for responsibly embedding AI into the ESH Management System while improving organizational performance, resilience, and long-term sustainability.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Additive manufacturing (AM), encompassing 3D and 4D printing, is transforming modern production by enabling the fabrication of lightweight, customized, and functional structures. Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into AM has introduced a new paradigm, enhancing design optimization, material discovery, predictive modeling, and real-time process control. AI-driven techniques, including machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), reinforcement learning (RL), and generative design, enable automated defect detection, process monitoring, and parameter optimization, significantly improving efficiency and quality. In 3D printing, AI supports personalized biomedical applications, lattice topology optimization, and high-accuracy patient-specific organ models, while in 4D printing, it facilitates the creation of stimuli-responsive, shape-morphing, and multifunctional structures using smart materials such as shape-memory polymers, hydrogels, and programmable composites. Furthermore, the emerging concept of 5D printing positions AI as the “fifth dimension,” enabling autonomous, adaptive, and sustainable manufacturing ecosystems through closed-loop control and generative design. Potential applications span biomedicine, aerospace, soft robotics, wearable technologies, and personalized healthcare. This chapter highlights how the convergence of AI, 3D/4D printing, and smart materials is driving the development of intelligent, adaptive, and resource-efficient manufacturing systems.

Modern cattle breeding increasingly integrates genomic selection (GS) with assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs) to accelerate genetic gain and enhance herd productivity. This review examines the synergistic application of GS and embryo-based technologies in dairy and beef cattle, and evaluates their potential to support precision breeding strategies. Relevant literature on genomic evaluation, embryo technologies and embryo-based breeding programs was synthesized to summarize current developments, opportunities, challenges, and global adoption patterns. ARTs, including artificial insemination, multiple ovulation and embryo transfer, in vitro embryo production, ovum pick-up, cryopreservation, and embryo biopsy, facilitate rapid multiplication of elite genetics and enable preimplantation selection. When combined with GS, these technologies allow estimation of genomic breeding values at early developmental stages, thereby reducing generation intervals, increasing selection intensity and improving the rate of genetic gain. Integrated breeding programs can also support targeted improvement of economically important traits (e.g. fertility, disease resistance, feed efficiency, production performance). Despite these advantages, practical implementation requires consideration of economic costs, technical expertise, infrastructure, recipient availability, and strategies to manage inbreeding and maintain genetic diversity. Global adoption varies considerably; highly integrated genomic and embryo-based breeding systems are well established in some countries (e.g. US, Australia) whereas emerging applications in regions including India, China, Brazil and Pakistan reflect varying levels of technological capacity and industry development. Emerging and developing approaches, including genome editing, artificial intelligence-assisted embryo evaluation and noninvasive embryo selection, together with continued improvements in established genomic prediction systems, are expected to further enhance precision breeding. Overall, integration of GS and ARTs represents a transformative approach for accelerating sustainable genetic improvement in cattle while supporting efficient and responsible breeding programs.
topics: Genetic and phenotypic traits in livestock

documents.abstract: This article analyzes nursing students' perceptions regarding the benefits, risks, and utility of artificial intelligence (AI) in their academic training and future professional practice. Through a narrative review of scientific literature published between 2020 and August 2026, the study examines AI's educational and clinical applications. The results reveal a generally favorable perception of AI, driven by its speed, accessibility, and ability to simplify complex concepts, summarize information, and facilitate autonomous learning. Furthermore, these tools can support clinical reasoning, case development, and the preparation of academic activities. However, risks are identified regarding incorrect information, algorithmic bias, privacy, academic integrity, technological dependence, and a potential decline in critical thinking. These concerns highlight the need to develop the digital, ethical, and professional competencies required to use these tools responsibly. The study concludes that the integration of AI into nursing must be planned, supervised, and person-centered. It is essential to verify information, protect data, and preserve clinical judgment, ensuring that technology complements but never replaces humanized care and the professional responsibility of nursing staff.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Substantive evidence related to barriers and enablers that impact the research activity of nurses and allied health professionals (AHPs) exists; however, less is known about the components and impact of interventions that influence research activity. This scoping review synthesizes empirical evidence on interventions designed to impact research activity among point-of-care nurses and AHPs within hospital and healthcare settings. METHODS: This scoping review was conducted in accordance with Arksey and O'Malley's framework. Primary, peer-reviewed studies describing an intervention focused on increasing research activity among postlicensure nurses and/or AHPs in CINAHL, Embase, and MEDLINE published between January 1, 2013, and May 2, 2024 were included. Abstracts and full texts were screened by 2 reviewers, and data extracted included study details, intervention details, and outcomes. RESULTS: Among the 43 studies that were included, interventions were commonly multicomponent, frequently coupled with education or training. Core components included research support, mentorship, collaborative activities, academic partnerships, and funding. Multicomponent, evidence-informed interventions were most frequently associated with research-related outcomes. Mentorship and protected time were consistently linked to addressing key persistent barriers, such as skill gaps and clinical workload. Sustained activity was commonly associated with intrinsic motivation and alignment with professional identity. CONCLUSIONS: Reported outcomes demonstrated improvements in individual research knowledge, skills, and confidence; strengthened organizational research culture and infrastructure; and increased individual and organizational research productivity. Healthcare organizations should consider implementing multicomponent interventions to increase research activity among point-of-care nurses and AHPs, recognizing that research-engaged clinicians are essential for evidence-based care and knowledge generation.

Additive manufacturing (AM) technologies have evolved from rapid prototyping to an indispensable part of modern production. Furthermore, recent advancements in the Internet of Things (IoT) have paved the way for creating intelligent, connected, and self-optimizing production environments within AM systems. This chapter addresses the creation of data-driven and intelligent manufacturing systems through the integration of IoT technologies into AM, highlighting the advantages of AM while drawing attention to control deficiencies in existing processes and proposing real-time monitoring of production parameters through sensors and connected systems. In addition, it elaborates on the ways real-time IoT monitoring systems can be built to enable on-site quality control, fault detection, and dynamic modification of production conditions. Therefore, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)-based algorithms are considered essential means for handling the huge amounts of data that IoT systems continually generate. Through these algorithms, one can optimize processes, predict faults, and enhance energy efficiency. Examples from the aerospace, biomedical, and small-batch manufacturing sectors show that IoT-enabled AM applications can fundamentally change the way accuracy, repeatability, and sustainability are handled.

Secure and Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) plays a pivotal role in strengthening technology-enabled Internet of Things and Internet of Medical Things (IoMT). This research work presents an innovative authentication frame 242 work based on electroencephalography (EEG) signals, leveraging their inherent ability to capture unique cognitive and neural patterns of individuals. Conventional mechanisms used in authentication often struggle in providing robust protection against sophisticated and evolving cyber threats in IoT and IoMT environments. To overcome these limitations, this study explores EEG-based authentication integrated with advanced machine learning and deep learning techniques. An extensive EEG dataset collected from participants performing diverse cognitive tasks is utilized to ensure variability and robustness.
