The proposed methodology employs a hybrid deep learning architecture that combines Convolutional Neural Networks for spatial feature extraction and Long Short-Term Memory networks for temporal dependency modeling, further enhanced through an autoencoder model for effective feature representation and dimensionality reduction. This integration enables accurate, resilient, and secure authentication. The results demonstrate the potential of EEG-driven biometric authentication as a secure and responsible AI solution, contributing to enhanced trust, privacy, and resilience in interconnected systems. Ongoing work focuses on refining the proposed models, improving computational efficiency, and validating their applicability in real-world IoT and IoMT deployment scenarios.

The article examines legal and ethical aspects of using artificial intelligence (AI) for genome editing, using the example of generating proteins used in genome editing using the CRISPR‑Cas method. It is shown that such proteins can be superior to natural ones, but they contain hundreds of mutations and insertions whose function is unknown, which creates unpredictable risks when they are used in medical practice. The author analyzes possible legal consequences: the liability of medical organizations to patients, the absence of recourse requirements for developers of AI products, the inadequacy of the existing regulation in Russia, and the need to strike a balance between innovation and safety. Measures to minimize risks are proposed, including independent testing, expanded informed consent, the creation of compensation funds, and data transparency.

topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Second-language acquisition (SLA) for non-cognate logographic languages—specifically Japanese across JLPT N5 through N1—suffers from historically high learner attrition. Kando Japanese (感動) introduces a full-stack, distributed pedagogical architecture synthesizing Krashen's Comprehensible Input (i+1) with a 250-story tiered Graded Reader (Tadoku), an interactive SVG vector-decomposition Kanji stroke engine (831 Joyo Kanji), a timezone-normalized SuperMemo SM-2 spaced repetition algorithm with intensity scheduling, and a contextual multi-LLM pedagogical companion (Sensei 3D) with deterministic semantic guardrails across 12 UI locales including Tamil and Hindi.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This research addresses the challenges SMEs in Santander face in adopting artificial intelligence, stemming from technological, organizational, and structural limitations that hinder its use as a tool for innovation and sustainable growth. The methodology focused on a comprehensive analysis of the benefits, barriers, and strategies associated with the responsible implementation of AI. Key findings revealed improvements in productivity, process optimization, cost reduction, enhanced decisionmaking, and greater business adaptability; however, obstacles persisted regarding inadequate technological infrastructure, a shortage of specialized talent, implementation costs, resistance to change, and a lack of trust in these technologies. The study concludes that AI can strengthen the innovation, competitiveness, and sustainability of SMEs, provided that its adoption integrates technological investment, workforce training, governance, and ethical principles
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: This essay undertakes a comparison between human intelligence and artificial intelligence (AI) in the legal field, arguing that the first possesses cognitive, epistemological, emotional and affective abilities that are crucial for jurists and that the second could never learn. Taking Carrie Menkel-Meadow’s teachings as the polestar, the essay will identify those fundamental abilities, analyse the features and limits of AI that make this latter incapable of learning such abilities, and finally make some suggestions on how we should develop the abilities at issue to lay down the foundations of a possible “Human Intelligence Project”. Keywords: human intelligence; artificial intelligence; legal professions; legal education; negotiation studies; legal skills; legal culture; nature of the law; conflict; dispute resolution.

Learner agency in L2 academic writing has taken on new significance with the rapid uptake of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools, raising questions about how agency is exercised in interaction with these tools and what pedagogical conditions support agentic and learning-oriented use. This study examined how 27 Japanese undergraduates in a 14-week English academic writing course exercised agency across three AI-permitted out-of-class essays, and how that agency related to the development of their unassisted writing. The course was designed around a pedagogical stance of teacher trust with two named elements: discretion granted to learners over their AI use, and a structure of explicit guidelines, AI literacy instruction, articulated principles, and weekly group discussions. Post-writing reflections (n = 81) were coded for the function of tool use and the quality of agency across seven facets, with substantial inter-rater reliability for both. Computational indices of lexical diversity, lexical sophistication, syntactic complexity, and accuracy were extracted from in-class AI-free pre- and post-essays, and Turnitin AI detection scores were recorded as research data, not as a policing instrument. Individual facets of agency were associated with different aspects of unassisted writing development: metacognitive awareness with differences in length, learning orientation with gains in lexical diversity, and critical evaluation with gains in clause density. Composite agency was not associated with development on any measure, supporting a dimensional view of agency in which facets carry different consequences for learning. Unassisted writing also shifted toward shorter, less subordinated clauses across the semester, a direction conventional measures of L2 syntactic development were not designed to detect. The findings support a view in which trust as a pedagogical condition shapes the forms of agency available to learners.

Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) is an important strategy for stroke prevention in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (AF) who have contraindications to long-term oral anticoagulation. We differentiate this review from existing literature by integrating recent controversial trial data and device-specific outcomes. Advances in technology and imaging have transformed LAAO into a widely adopted percutaneous therapy. Large trials and registries demonstrate LAAO’s non-inferiority to oral anticoagulants. For example, the PRAGUE-17 trial (N=402) found LAAO non-inferior to direct oral anticoagulants, while PROTECT-AF and PREVAIL 5-year data (N=1114) showed significant reductions in hemorrhagic stroke. The surgical LAAOS III trial (N=4811) demonstrated a 33% longterm reduction in stroke or systemic embolism. Major complications have declined; the SURPASS registry (N=16,446) demonstrated a 0.51% incidence of pericardial effusion for the WATCHMAN FLX. In the Amulet IDE trial, pericardial effusion occurred in 2.4% of Amulet patients versus 1.2% of WATCHMAN patients. Recent 2026 NEJM trials (CHAMPION-AF and CLOSURE-AF) reached opposite conclusions in different populations, remaining a central controversy. Emerging technologies like artificial intelligence-guided planning, which accurately predicted device size in 72.7% of cases, and low-thrombogenic devices continue to improve safety. This review summarizes contemporary techniques, imaging, complications, outcomes, and future directions.

The purpose of this article is to help students prepare for job offer negotiations. Although resources to help students practice job offer negotiations exist, these activities primarily use peer role-play and may be constrained by synchronous scheduling and limited individualized feedback. We present a fully customizable artificial intelligence negotiation chatbot that supplements, rather than replaces, peer role-play. The exercise provides late undergraduate and graduate students with a low-stakes, repeatable setting in which to rehearse job offer negotiation preparation, requests, and responses at their own pace while receiving individualized feedback. Because chatbot practice does not reproduce the nonverbal communication, reciprocal interpersonal responses, perspective-taking, and relationship-management demands of a human negotiation partner, instructors should use the exercise alongside peer role-play and related human interaction.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT The growth of e‐commerce and the corresponding increase in the number of online reviews have driven the demand for recommender systems that capture user preferences. Online reviews contain detailed evaluations of item aspects, and recent studies have employed aspect‐based sentiment analysis (ABSA) to incorporate fine‐grained user sentiment for improved personalisation. However, existing ABSA‐based recommendation approaches rely on predefined aspect categories, which prevents them from capturing user preferences for specific aspect terms and limits their generalisation across diverse domains. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel ABSA‐based recommendation framework, domain‐agnostic aspect‐aware recommendation (DAAR), which leverages large language models (LLMs) to extract aspect terms and integrate them with sentiment information. First, aspect terms that represent the targets of user evaluation are extracted from review texts using LLMs. Then, semantic representations of the aspect terms are generated using Phrase‐BERT based on bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT), and sentiment scores for each aspect term are obtained through a sentiment analysis model based on decoding‐enhanced BERT with disentangled attention (DeBERTa). Finally, the two representations are combined into a unified representation, and an attention mechanism is applied to capture the relative importance among aspect terms. The resulting representation is then integrated with user–item interactions to predict the final rating. Experimental results on the Yelp and Amazon review datasets demonstrate that DAAR outperforms the baseline models and shows strong generalisation capabilities. This indicates that the proposed framework alleviates domain dependency and more precisely captures user preferences by integrating users' sentiment towards aspect terms.

In the recent past, mapping technologies have developed very fast, moving from 2D to 3D, and static mapping to real-time mapping. These technologies include photogrammetry, remote sensing, Global Positioning System, drones/unmanned aerial vehicles, Light Detection and Ranging, and Geographic Information System (GIS). We not only get faster results but also higher accuracy of mapping. This chapter discusses the role of these technologies in efficiently mapping the land surface. These mapping technologies have revolutionized the collection of land surface data/information, and their subsequent analysis using the capabilities of GIS. The 3D models, such as Digital Elevation Model and Digital Surface Model, can be generated, which are required for the planning, design, construction, management, and monitoring of land resources. The integration of these technologies with the capabilities of artificial intelligence) and machine learning enables automatic terrain mapping, and real-time monitoring of an area.

Abstract Rare earth elements (REEs) are designated as critical materials due to their urgent need and supply uncertainties. The scarcity of REE supply is exacerbated by environmentally damaging extraction practices, necessitating more efficient, sustainable extraction and separation methods. Traditional techniques such as solvent extraction are often constrained by their extensive organic solvent consumption and limited extraction efficiency, especially for e-waste feedstocks containing heterogeneous compositions. As an alternative to traditional methods, solid-phase extraction (SPE) technique streamlines REE extraction and separation by providing high chelating selectivity, fewer operational stages, and minimal secondary waste generation. This review explores recent advances in ligand design for REE recovery, especially carbonyl amide-based, phosphorus-containing, β-diketone- and acylpyrazolone-based, macrocyclic, and biologically derived ligands. Enhancing the surface density of more REE-selective ligands on solid-phase matrices provides a viable pathway to overcome the thermodynamic constraints of separating adjacent, chemically homologous REEs in urban mining processes. Direct applications of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), to experimentally validated REE recovery remain limited and are mainly focused on narrowly defined tasks, including metal–ligand stability-constant prediction, ligand ranking, extraction-equilibrium modeling, and process simulation. Rather than treating AI-assisted REE recovery as a mature field, this review critically distinguishes demonstrated REE-specific applications from transferable computational frameworks that remain to be validated. Particular attention is given to molecular descriptors, coordination geometry, thermodynamic properties, data quality, and validation requirements for predictive ligand design. By connecting established REE coordination chemistry with emerging AI methodologies, this review identifies current limitations and proposes a chemically grounded roadmap for future ligand discovery and process optimization.

An inaccurate response to an ambiguous prompt can reflect a mistaken interpretation, an unsupported factual assertion or a translation problem. These outcomes require different explanations and evaluation criteria. This paper examines their relationship through a structured literature analysis and a proposed Chinese-English evaluation of GPT and Claude models. It distinguishes ambiguity in meaning and reference from factual support, translation fidelity and the adequacy of available evidence. Existing studies inform a comparative framework, while their different models, languages and tasks limit direct comparisons. The proposed evaluation pairs ambiguous prompts with disambiguated versions and contrasts implicit cultural context with explicit context. Bilingual reviewers validate the materials before generation. Exact model versions, prompting conditions and output records are retained, and blinded human annotation separates supported claims, confirmed contradictions, unsupported additions and unresolved cases. Evaluation reports factual outcomes alongside answer coverage, clarification and abstention, with repeated outputs analysed at the item level. Mitigation involves clarifying consequential uncertainty, supplying relevant context and checking claims against appropriate sources. The paper contains no new model outputs, measured hallucination rates or model rankings. Its contribution is a design for examining how language and context affect interpretation and factual reporting without treating every incorrect or unscorable response as hallucination.

As human–artificial intelligence (AI) romantic relationships become increasingly prevalent, understanding how they develop is important. Such relationships differ from human–human relationships in how AI partners accommodate user needs and preferences, potentially influencing relationship development and closeness. In this survey ( N = 167), individuals who reported falling in love more quickly with human partners also tended to do so with AI partners. However, paired within-subject analyses ( n = 110) revealed that participants perceived a faster overall pace of falling in love with AI than human partners, driven primarily by shorter conversation lengths rather than fewer days or total conversations. Despite this expediency, participants reported greater current relational closeness with human partners than AI partners. Perceived similarity with AI partners was positively associated with relational closeness and relationship quality with AI. These findings suggest that human–AI romantic relationships may develop rapidly through familiar interpersonal processes such as similarity attraction, yet involve lower relational closeness.

Objective: To develop and evaluate machine learning (ML) models to predict clinical pregnancy (CP) outcomes in couples with unexplained infertility (UI) undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF), thereby enhancing early treatment decision-making and patient counseling. Materials and Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 145 couples diagnosed with UI and treated at a single-center IVF clinic. Live birth data were not available; therefore, CP was used as the primary outcome. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory parameters were collected, and five ML algorithms-light gradient boosting machine (LGBM), random forest, logistic regression, extra trees classifier, and eXtreme gradient boosting-were applied to predict CP outcomes. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Permutation-based feature importance analysis was performed to identify key predictive variables. Results: Among the evaluated models, the LGBM model achieved the highest test-set ROC-AUC (0.712) and an accuracy of 65.2%. Given the small test sample and the lack of external validation, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory. Variables receiving the highest permutation feature-importance scores included total gonadotropin dose, initial gonadotropin dose, total sperm count, progressive motile sperm count, and infertility duration. These findings should be interpreted as exploratory and do not establish that these variables are independent predictors of CP. Conclusion: This study presents the first ML-based approach tailored to predicting CP outcomes in couples with UI undergoing IVF. The results highlight the potential of artificial intelligence to inform personalized reproductive care. These exploratory findings demonstrate the feasibility of applying ML methods in UI. Larger prospective multicenter studies are required to determine whether clinically useful prediction models can be developed.
topics: Assisted Reproductive Technology and Twin Pregnancy

documents.abstract: Abstract Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) has emerged as a detection tool to ensure food safety and quality, especially for the rapid and accurate identification of adulterants. However, its application is challenged by limitations of commercial matrices, such as high background interference and low sensitivity. Complex sample preparation, labor-intensive data processing, and human errors further hinder its adoption in high-throughput workflows. Unlike previous reviews that primarily draw horizontal comparisons between MALDI-TOF MS and other conventional food detection methods, this review centers on complementary technical strategies to overcome the intrinsic analytical limitations of MALDI-TOF MS. It assesses innovative matrix materials for improved small-molecule detection performance. This work also provides a critical discussion of microfluidic-enabled automated sample preparation and machine learning-assisted spectral interpretation, which target current bottlenecks and expand practical applicability. The combination of MALDI-TOF MS with cutting-edge technologies provides promising new opportunities toward precise, automated, and high-throughput capabilities in food analysis.

Background/objectives This study examines how human listeners and automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems process speech under varying background noise levels. Methods Three groups of human participants—normal-sighted (NSLs), blind (BLs), and hearing-impaired listeners (HILs)—were compared with two state-of-the-art ASR systems, Whisper and TurboScribe. Forty Arabic sentences (20 imperative, 20 interrogative) were presented at four signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs: +10, +5, −5, −10 dB) using passenger boarding noise to simulate realistic acoustic environments. Results Accuracy declined with increasing noise for all groups, although rates varied substantially. BLs performed best, maintaining 85% accuracy even at −10 dB SNR, whereas HILs showed the steepest decline. The ASR systems achieved near-human performance in moderate noise but degraded sharply under severe masking, mirroring HIL trends. Statistical analysis confirmed significant group differences across SNRs ( p < 0.05). A linear mixed-effects analysis further revealed a significant advantage for interrogative over imperative sentences in human listeners ( p < 0.05), plausibly attributable to the rich prosodic cues of question intonation, but no comparable benefit was observed for ASR systems ( p = 0.30), which appear to weight segmental over prosodic information. Conclusion These findings highlight that, although contemporary ASR models approach human performance in favorable conditions, they lack the adaptive mechanisms that allow humans—especially BLs—to sustain intelligibility in complex acoustic scenes. By situating ASR performance within the spectrum of human auditory variability, this research underscores both the progress and the limitations of machine hearing and points toward neurobiologically inspired strategies for achieving noise-robust speech recognition. Clinically, this framework suggests that benchmarking ASR systems against the full spectrum of human auditory variability—including hearing-impaired and blind listeners—can inform the design of accessibility tools, hearing-aid signal processing, and supplementary diagnostic measures of speech-in-noise perception in audiology practice.

Abstract Gender, agency, and objectification are important dimensions of how participants and relationships are represented in poetry, yet their systematic study in Arabic verse remains difficult because meaning is often conveyed through metaphor, ellipsis, compressed syntax, and context-dependent relations. This study investigates how gendered agency and objectification are represented across a large corpus of Arabic poetry and examines whether computational analysis can capture these literary-semantic relations while preserving textual evidence and interpretive uncertainty. A neuro-symbolic computational framework was developed to represent participants, events, agency, gender representation, and objectification as explicit, evidence-linked semantic relations. Large language model extraction was combined with formal constraint validation and expert adjudication. Evaluated against an expert-annotated sample of 4,500 verses, automated semantic extraction achieved an F1-score of 0.884 on the hold-out test set. Following evaluation and targeted adjudication within the annotated sample, the resulting constraint-guided pipeline was applied across 31,209 single-verse poems spanning twelve historical periods and eight poetic genres. Corpus-level analysis identified distinct distributions in gendered agency: male-coded participants were classified as active in 61.8\% of agency-related instances, compared with 48.2\% for female-coded participants, while the latter showed higher proportions of reactive and passive involvement. Objectification was distributed across multiple forms, with symbolic objectification emerging as the most frequent category (38.4\%), exceeding direct physical objectification (21.6\%). These results make recurrent patterns of gendered literary representation systematically inspectable at corpus scale while retaining links to textual evidence, ambiguity, and provenance. Ultimately, the study demonstrates how evidence-grounded computational methods can support large-scale investigation of literary representation while retaining interpretive boundaries.

The present study focuses on methods for supporting the orientation of blind and visually impaired people within public buildings. Various innovative navigation solutions are reviewed, including principal mapping approaches and systems based on artificial intelligence. Based on the identified challenges and the specific needs of visually impaired users, the authors propose the development of tactile maps incorporating Braille labels in accordance with an established standard. A tactile floor plan of a building was developed using Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM), 3D-printing technology featuring marked locations and dimensions that comply with standard requirements. The selected method offers rapid production at relatively low cost, thereby facilitating the mapping of a larger number of public buildings. Future work will include an analysis and evaluation of the map’s tactile usability and suitability for practical application.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: This exploratory study examines artificial intelligence anxiety among academic librarians in the United Arab Emirates, a multilingual context undergoing rapid digital transformation. A cross-sectional online survey of 72 academic library professionals, recruited through purposive and snowball sampling, employed a newly developed 35-item instrument covering seven conceptually derived dimensions: job role evolution, ethical and bureaucratic concerns, patron resistance and social trust, governance and strategic alignment, infrastructure and digital divide, vendor and sustainability, and linguistic and cultural anxiety. Internal consistency ranged from acceptable to strong (α = 0.774–0.898). Overall, AI anxiety was moderate (M = 3.33 on a five-point scale), with ethical and bureaucratic concerns (M = 3.47), infrastructure and digital divide (M = 3.42), and vendor and sustainability concerns (M = 3.36) recording the highest means. However, the narrow range across construct means (0.23 points) warrants treating these differences as descriptive rather than substantive rankings. Concerns about storing patron data on foreign servers and shortages of skilled staff received the highest item-level ratings. Although women reported higher scores across all seven dimensions, no gender or other demographic differences remained statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. The findings highlight the institutional, infrastructural, ethical and governance conditions associated with AI anxiety in academic libraries. The proposed dimensions offer a context-specific framework for further investigation, subject to validation in larger samples. Practical implications include developing localized and multilingual AI tools, expanding inclusive professional development, and strengthening participatory governance of AI procurement and policy.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This registration describes a scoping review that will systematically map the evidence on clinical decision support systems (CDSSs) used by nurses and other clinicians in intensive care and emergency triage settings, with particular attention to reverse triage during disaster surges. The review will identify CDSS types, functionalities, and impacts on decision‑making time, accuracy, confidence, and cognitive workload, construct an evidence gap map across CDSS types and clinical contexts, and develop the CDSS‑RT conceptual framework to guide future CDSS‑assisted reverse triage system design and implementation.

Purpose This study maps the knowledge domain of internal control and information technology (IC-IT) and traces how the intellectual foundations, thematic evolution and future research agenda of IC have evolved alongside digital technologies. The theoretical implications of these descriptive patterns are discussed for future theory development. Design/methodology/approach Using CiteSpace, the study analyses 1,222 publications and 43,092 cited references from the Web of Science Core Collection for 2005–2025. It conducts reference co-citation, author, country and institutional collaboration, cited journal, keyword co-occurrence and subject category analyses. Findings The findings show that IC-IT research has evolved from compliance-oriented IC, risk management and internal audit toward technology-enabled and intelligent control systems. The field is grounded in accounting, auditing, information systems and management, with emerging themes including artificial intelligence, machine learning, blockchain, cloud computing, access control, audit automation and real-time monitoring. Originality/value This study conceptualizes IC-IT as an integrated interdisciplinary domain and provides the first full-domain bibliometric mapping that crosses four traditionally isolated research streams. It identifies a three-stage evolution from compliance-oriented control toward technology-embedded and intelligent governance, showing how digital technologies are reorienting internal-control research toward new objectives, mechanisms, audit evidence and accountability systems.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed the educational landscape through personalized learning, automated assessment, and expanded access to information; however, it has simultaneously raised ethical issues such as cognitive dependency, the erosion of academic integrity, algorithmic bias, digital attachment, and the weakening of pedagogical relationships. This study aims to analyze the impact of AI on human dignity in education and to outline the direction of its application based on the perspective of Catholic Social Teaching. A qualitative library research method was employed, utilizing content analysis and a critical-hermeneutic approach to examine documents from the Catholic Church's Magisterium and reputable scholarly journals. The findings indicate that the application of AI risks reducing learners to mere computational data and eroding their moral autonomy. The principles of human dignity (Imago Dei), the common good (bonum commune), subsidiarity, solidarity, and social justice prove relevant as an interpretive framework for positioning AI as an instrumental tool that serves integral human development.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Smart orthopedic implants have evolved significantly in recent times. These implants are designed to address the limitations of traditional implants and allow for superior outcomes. This chapter evaluates the historical progression, current state-of-the-art technologies, and future directions in this field. The chapter shows the transition from inert mechanical devices to active systems. The chapter then focuses on the key materials and manufacturing techniques that make implants “intelligent.” Various smart materials such as shape-memory alloys (SMAs) and smart polymers that can sense and respond to physiological changes and can be used for drug delivery and controlled degradation have been discussed. The chapter also details manufacturing processes like additive manufacturing (AM) that allow for the creation of intricate, patient-specific geometries with integrated sensor networks and drug reservoirs. These innovations are crucial for theranostics, a novel approach that combines therapy and diagnostics. The chapter also discusses the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning for real-time data analysis and personalized treatment. The potential for bio-integrated electronics, self-powered implants, and fully biodegradable systems is also explored. This chapter also provides a perspective on the potential of smart implants in revolutionizing orthopedic implants from passive implants to active, intelligent, and personalized interventions.

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support decision-making in high-stakes domains, where a model's risk preference, its tendency to favor lower-risk or higher-risk options under uncertainty, can shape the decisions it supports. Prior studies measuring these preferences in LLMs have produced mixed results. Several used fixed designs, such as choice lists, which locate the point where a preference changes only as finely as their preset values allow. Adaptive procedures, which adjust each query to earlier responses, concentrate measurement near that point and are established for eliciting human risk preferences. We present such a procedure for LLMs: it poses a choice between a lower-risk and a higher-risk option, varies the expected value of the higher-risk option across steps, locates by binary search the model's tipping point, the point at which its outputs shift to favor the higher-risk option, and reports it as an index of risk preference under one probability structure. We applied the procedure to eight LLMs from four providers (OpenAI, San Francisco, CA, USA; Anthropic, San Francisco, CA, USA; Google, Mountain View, CA, USA; xAI, Palo Alto, CA, USA), using emergency and disaster management vignettes, and tested whether presenting each option's expected value explicitly, rather than leaving it to be inferred, changed the measured preference. Median tipping points for six of the eight models fell near the point of equal expected value under both presentations. Claude Sonnet 4.6's tipping point was higher when the expected value was left to be inferred, with a shift whose bootstrap interval excludes 0; Claude Haiku 4.5's was higher as a point estimate, but its shift interval includes 0. In individual queries, deviations from expected-value maximization concentrated in four models: those of the two Anthropic models all toward the lower-risk option and those of the two Google models almost all toward the higher-risk option. Over the range queried in both presentations, presenting the expected value explicitly reduced these deviations in all four models. Because the two presentations convey the same expected values, the reduction indicates that these models did not respond to them as equivalent. The procedure applies to any model accessible via a text interface and is a reusable tool for comparing and screening models for risk-related decision support.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Crime-reporting mobile applications can enhance community safety and engagement in urban areas, yet their adoption remains low, partly because developers prioritize technological features over residents' social realities. This study used an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design to identify and validate the sociotechnical factors that drive adoption. Two focus groups and an analysis of 660 app reviews revealed that users' initial sense of usefulness fades, whereas sustained engagement depends on perceived value (PV), comprising six dimensions: safety, anonymity, recency, autonomy, camaraderie, and accessibility. A survey of 505 urban residents, analyzed with PLS-SEM, validated PV as a formative higher-order construct formed by four of these dimensions (safety, anonymity, autonomy, and camaraderie). PV was the strongest predictor of behavioral intention, ahead of effort expectancy, facilitating conditions, and performance expectancy, and behavioral intention strongly predicted actual use. The model explained 75% of the variance in behavioral intention and 51% in actual use. The findings offer design principles for community-centered crime-reporting technologies.

Purpose This study aims to examine the strategic mechanisms women entrepreneurs use to navigate systemic barriers and drive sustainable, inclusive social impact, integrating the entrepreneurial feminism framework (EFF) and the theory of grit (TOG). Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a qualitative, longitudinal single-case design combining literature review, real-time case analysis of the STREE initiative by Kshamata Innovation Foundation (KIF) in India, and abductive reasoning. Data were drawn from interviews with founders, employees, supporters and beneficiaries, four annual STREE closure reports (2021–2024) and beneficiary case-study documentation, analyses through thematic coding and strategy mapping. Findings Nine literature derived strategies are validated and organised into three domains: Financial literacy, intrinsic motivation and empowerment strategies (S1–S3) included in Motivation and Agency; Multilevel interventions, financial access and networking encompassed under Support System (S4–S6); and human capital transformation, frugal innovation and entrepreneurial ecosystem (S7–S9) comprised under Innovation. The resulting GRIT-EQ framework demonstrates how feminist values and psychological grit combine to sustain impact-driven entrepreneurship under adversity. Practical implications The study offers actionable insights for practitioners, policymakers, government and NGOs to design gender inclusive programs, simplify funding processes and build resilient and supportive entrepreneurial ecosystems. Originality/value This study offers one of the first longitudinal, practice-based accounts of how a women-led Indian social enterprise builds pathways for beneficiaries to grow in a gender-unequal market, extending EFF and grit research into an operational roadmap aligned with SDGs 1, 5 and 10.

of dire ecological threats? We examine four systemic barriers behind collective inertia and argue that collective sustainability agency is necessary to overcome systemic inertia. Collective sustainability agency is the organizational capacity through which members transform individual sustainability concerns and responsibilities into coordinated collective influence over the practices, priorities, and structures that shape organizational sustainability outcomes. Unlike collective efficacy or organizational climate, which centers on shared beliefs about a group's capability, collective sustainability agency emphasizes the mobilization and exercise of that capability. Building on Wong et al.'s (2025) call to recognize employees as collective agents of systemic sustainability change, this perspective focuses on how organizations transform dispersed individual attitudes into shared responsibility, coordinated action, and collective influence capable of challenging organizational inertia.Environmental sustainability is defined as practices that minimize ecological harm, conserve natural resources, and support long-term ecological balance (Ones & Dilchert, 2012). While employees may personally endorse these principles, they often engage in environmentally harmful practices at work. This discrepancy occurs because organizational structures, incentives, leadership, and daily job demands shape human behavior far more powerfully than personal attitudes alone. Addressing the "attitude-behavior gap" requires more than changing individual minds-it demands the deliberate design of organizational systems that actively motivate, support, and mobilize sustainable choices (Kühner et al., 2025).Most organizations operate with economic success as their central priority. This creates a "growth paradox," where environmental sustainability and economic expansion are viewed as diametrically opposed tradeoffs (Edwards, 2021). In many corporate cultures, taking a sustainable stance is incorrectly equated with stagnation rather than progress (Amel et al., 2026).Research examining the economic-environmental relationship has yielded nuanced patterns of results. Fernandes et al. (2021) found that sustainability innovations and green technology transfers supported economic growth without harming financial performance. Meta-analytic results also showed a consistent, positive, bidirectional relationship between sustainability and organizational profit (Dixon-Fowler et al., 2013). Integrating sustainability into strategic planning was associated with higher stock prices, lower risks, and fewer unplanned environmental cleanup costs. Organizational longevity also positively correlated with proactive environmental investments (Ones et al., 2026). This relationship, however, has several moderators. Costa and Opare (2025) found that organizations with higher production volumes, older equipment and processes, and aggressive dividend payouts generated significantly higher levels of toxic chemical releases than those with lower production volumes, newer equipment and processes, and less aggressive payouts. Rahi et al. (2024) identified other contextual moderators in that financial return on green initiatives was strengthened when organizations had gender-diverse boards, tied executive compensation to ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) metrics, possessed ample slack resources, and answered to sustainability-minded investors. A negative relationship was found for companies, markets, and investors operating within highly capitalist frameworks--such as the United States, the United Kingdom, and Ireland that "historically undervalued or ignored green practices" (p. 812) while prioritizing short-term financial returns.When looking at the country level, Teixeira et al. (2025) compared the world's 10 most sustainable and 10 least sustainable countries, arguing that macroeconomic growth is a primary driver for environmental compliance. They suggested companies become more capable of implementing green practices upon acquiring financial and institutional resources. Contradicting this argument, however, is evidence that high-income nations contribute disproportionately to climate extremes (Schöngart et al., 2025), using six times more resources and generating ten times the per capita climate impact than low-income nations (UNEP, 2024). In short, macrostructural factors shape the sustainability-profit relationship, constraining the impact of individual action and creating pressures that can undermine the perceived value of sustainability and discourage organizations from pursuing green strategies.Many capitalist economies adopt a short-term orientation, prioritizing immediate financial returns while discounting future risks and liabilities. Because markets reward quarterly earnings improvements, executives work to keep immediate operational costs low. This induces a bias where the visible, upfront cost of sustainability initiatives loom larger than the abstract, back-end cost of future environmental degradation. This behavior aligns closely with prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). Organizational leadership places a disproportionate psychological value on avoiding immediate losses (the outof-pocket expenses of green investments) while discounting delayed gains and future penalties. Because the long-term consequences of environmental neglect are often delayed, distributed, or uncertain, the immediate cost of prevention feels like a loss.Furthermore, even when short-term decisions result in eventual ecological disaster, the organization itself rarely bears the full financial burden. The costs of degraded water tables, polluted land, and declining public health are externalized onto the public. This moral hazard fosters an organizational mindset of grabbing immediate payoffs under the assumption that the current leadership will no longer be around when the environmental bill comes due. While institutions gravitate toward crisis management and instant gratification, long-term operational horizons are ultimately more effective.Sustainability remains a low corporate priority due to diffused responsibility and a lack of accountability. Because the degradation of our climate is a collective, slow-moving crisis, no single entity shoulders the blame. Future remedial costs are spread across taxpayers, governments, local communities, and future generations. This systemic inertia is further compounded by socio-political rhetoric. Framing sustainability through an ideological lens (e.g., dismissing climate science as a hoax) or characterizing environmental protections as inherently onerous and economically destructive supports justifying the status quo.Organizations must navigate domestic and international governmental regulations. Proactive companies integrate sustainability into their overarching corporate strategy to stay ahead of the legislative curve. Conversely, adopting a purely reactive stance results in defensive, "quick-fix" adjustments that require expensive retooling and structural redesigns. Furthermore, basic compliance often misses the competitive advantages-such as reduced energy, water, and material costs-offered by strategic, sustainable innovation.External regulations can be a risky path. In an experimental simulation, Baxter and Pelletier (2020) observed that introducing regulatory sanctions increased sustainable behaviors only while those sanctions were actively enforced. Once the threat of penalties was removed, sustainable behaviors plummeted. This aligns directly with self-determination theory: actions driven solely by compliance cease when the external threat disappears, while actions driven by internal values become self-sustaining. Sustainability implementation, however, presents organizations with complex and competing demands. Strategies for advancing sustainability can involve substantial implementation costs, uncertain financial returns, competing stakeholder pressures, and political and regulatory constraints. These challenges are very real and can reinforce organizational inertia, particularly when short-term financial priorities compete with longer-term environmental goals. Navigating these tensions requires more than individual commitment to sustainability; it requires an organizational architecture that bridges individual will for sustainability with the collective capacity to make it happen. Such an architecture can transform dispersed sustainability concerns into coordinated action, enabling organizations to overcome systemic barriers and embed sustainability within the structures and practices that guide organizational decision making.Similar to Wong, et al (2026), we propose that to overcome collective inaction, organizations must build collective agency through actively initiating change, challenging institutional norms, and transforming the systemic structures that govern them. Cultivating collective agency requires an overhaul of an organization's culture, in particular its underlying norms and assumptions.According to the theory of reasoned action (Fishbein & Ajzen, 1975;2010), subjective norms are primary determinants of individual behavioral choices. Within a corporate culture, these norms manifest in two ways:• Normative Beliefs: Signaling what an organization values most-its core priorities and idealized behaviors. These beliefs stem from deeply embedded, unexamined assumptions that implicitly drive employee actions without conscious awareness. • Motivation to Comply: Reflecting an employee's evaluation of the positive and negative outcomes resulting from their compliance.Social norms powerfully dictate accepted workplace behavior. Individual employees find it exceedingly difficult to defy an established corporate culture. A lone worker championing an environmental agenda can feel isolated and fear a substantial professional cost as superiors and peers may view time and energy spent on green initiatives as wasted or counter to the organization's capitalist motives (Amel et al., 2023). Leaders are statistically more likely to empower conformist employees who reinforce traditional values rather than those perceived as "rocking the boat" (Smith et al., 2026).We argue that to mobilize collective sustainability agency, organizations must develop and encourage norms that embed sustainability in their culture through planned change, executive accountability, GHRM, and job design (Figure 1).Shifting an organization's core trajectory relies heavily on collective human effort. This transition cannot be derivative; it must be a radical, macro-level transformation, as minor adjustments can easily be bypassed or ignored.Undertaking comprehensive culture change is difficult, as individuals naturally resist disruption in favor of the status quo. Lewin's (1951) three-stage model of planned change provides a framework to navigate this friction. The first stage, unfreezing, calls for the disruption of automated, habitual routines forcing employees out of "autopilot." The next stage implements new sustainable processes and systems. Finally, the last stage, refreezing, solidifies and integrates the changes into daily operations and corporate identity mitigating resistance. Macrostructural shifts maximize ecological returns (IPCC, 2023). For example, while an individual can consciously choose to flip off a light switch, an organization that installs motion-sensor lighting across all facilities scales that positive behavior a thousand-fold.To achieve radical cultural change, we suggest that organizations target two foundational value shifts:• Shifting to a long-term frame of reference: Ignoring sustainability may generate temporary, upfront financial gains, but invites catastrophic long-term liabilities. The cumulative cost of environmental remediation frequently dwarfs the initial cost of prevention. A prime example is General Electric (GE), which discharged PCBs into the Hudson River from the 1940s to the 1970s. GE's long-term management costs are projected to exceed $2 billion, encompassing dredging, litigation, fines, and penaltiesalongside intangible damages like stricter regulatory oversight, eroded investor confidence, and severe brand devaluation (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2013). • Embracing a purpose-driven transformation: Prioritizing long-term viability over quarterly performance can create conditions that may enhance organizational flexibility and resilience. Such a shift may also provide strategic advantages by encouraging innovation, strengthening long-term performance, and mitigating systemic risks (Ones et al., 2026). Organizations that neglect sustainability may face escalating operating costs due to the finite nature of natural resources-including water, clean air, rare earth minerals, energy, and arable land. Without deliberate corporate intervention to protect and replenish resources, supply chains may face disruptions and cost increases that could undermine long-term profitability. Early sustainability adopters may be uniquely positioned as leaders in emerging green markets, which represent some of the fastestgrowing sectors of the global economy (World Economic Forum, 2025).A pro-environmental culture fosters higher employee engagement, deeper institutional commitment, and greater job satisfaction (Amel et al., 2023). When an organization's norms embrace green values, even employees who were initially indifferent are often swept along.Employees internalize these values voluntarily, moving beyond behavioral compliance to true psychological commitment.A corporate reputation rooted in genuine environmental stewardship acts as a powerful magnet for stakeholders. Meta-analytic evidence confirms that modern consumers are willing to pay a premium for sustainably produced goods (Tully & Winer, 2014). In contrast, "greenwashing"providing lip service to environmental initiatives without taking genuine action (Walker & Wan, 2012)-shatters consumer trust and may result in institutional investors divesting their support.Radical systemic change must be initiated from the top. CEOs and corporate boards determine how internal resources are deployed, balancing external market pressures and regulatory demands against internal structural constraints (Ones et al., 2026). Notably, a global survey revealed that 98% of CEOs now view it as their explicit responsibility to make their organizations sustainable-a 15% increase over the preceding decade (United Nations & Accenture, 2023).This top-down alignment is critical because employee eco-initiatives are directly tied to the visible actions of their leaders (Katz et al., 2022;Zacher et al., 2024). The personal convictions of top executives establish baseline behavioral norms for the entire enterprise. When evaluating the antecedents of employee workplace behavior, research shows that a supportive green climate combined with explicit pro-environmental leadership provides the necessary psychological safety for workers to manifest their personal values. Ultimately, corporate leadership behaviors function as highly visible, observable benchmarks that increase the salience of an employee's own internal ethical standards (Zhao et al., 2026). To facilitate this clarity, leadership must establish explicit operational rules and clear behavioral choices (Oettingen & Gollwitzer, 2026), building collective sustainability efficacy across the workforce.HRM professionals are vital strategic partners in translating corporate vision into daily practice (Westerman et al., 2020). By embedding sustainability into core personnel processes, HRM drives employee behavior through how roles are defined, who is recruited, and how talent is evaluated and rewarded (Podgorodnichenko et al., 2022;Zacher et al., 2023).Schneider's Attraction-Selection-Attrition (ASA) Model (1987) suggests that the mechanism for this cultural evolution involves:• Proactively marketing the firm's green initiatives to attract candidates with matching values,• Hiring individuals whose personal ethics align with the organization's sustainability goals, • Retaining those who thrive in a green culture, while misaligned individuals exit over time.By hiring for value congruence, organizations shift employees away from reactive compliance toward intrinsic motivation (Ones et al., 2026). Rather than viewing sustainability as an external regulatory threat, workers perceive it as an opportunity for personal growth, well-being, engagement, and meaningful performance.While macro-level organizational outcomes are not directly under an individual worker's control, their immediate task behaviors are. Green job design structurally integrates environmental targets into everyday routines, establishing clear benchmarks for feedback and performance rewards.When sustainability is a built-in feature of a job description rather than an optional afterthought, it establishes clear expectations and personal accountability for ecological outcomes (Katz & Stuhlmacher, 2026).Much of the sustainability literature treats individual and structural change as separate pathways to sustainability, emphasizing either changes in individual attitudes and behaviors or changes in organizational systems. Individuals, however, often face systemic inertia that constrains their ability to challenge and transform entrenched systems. We argue that organizational structures must enable and reinforce individual sustainability attitudes for them to translate into meaningful sustainability change. Transforming individual sustainability concerns into shared responsibility enables collective sustainability agency to mobilize the capacity to overcome systemic inertia and drive meaningful organizational sustainability change. As collective agents of environmental sustainability, organizational members can challenge an economic paradigm that prioritizes short-term gains over long-term environmental health. We propose that collective sustainability agency positions organizations and their members as active stewards of environmental protection, empowering them to create the conditions for enduring environmental sustainability. By restructuring organizational cultures to foster collective sustainability agency, organizations can cultivate a shared responsibility to the planet while potentially enhancing their capacity for agility, resilience, and long-term sustainability. Achieving this transformation requires corporate leaders and stakeholders to move beyond incrementalism, embrace systemic change, and create the conditions in which sustainable behavior becomes the organizational norm.

Admission offices in Indian colleges handle a large volume of repetitive enquiries about eligibility, fees, documents and Centralized Admission Process (CAP) rounds, and conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed to absorb this load. This paper reviews fifteen works covering educational chatbots, university and admission assistants, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), hallucination and abstention in large language models (LLMs), speech recognition, human-AI interaction guidelines and data-protection law. The review finds that educational chatbots are well studied for learning and FAQ support, and that retrieval reduces hallucination in generated answers. However, admission-facing systems rarely control which knowledge is allowed into answers, rarely decline when a candidate-specific record is missing, seldom model consent for personalised outreach, and do not distinguish drafted or simulated actions from real communication. Based on these gaps, the paper proposes a human-in-the-loop framework with four mechanisms: an approval-gated knowledge lifecycle, verified-record grounding with explicit abstention for CAP queries, a consent gate before any personalised message, and an explicit action-state model that labels drafts, previews and blocked actions. The framework is presented as a design proposal together with evaluation criteria for grounding, abstention, consent enforcement and record completeness, to guide future pilot studies in admission offices.

documents.abstract: In the context of a digital transformation that is fundamentally refining the nature of work and leadership dynamics, this research examines the mediating role of job engagement and the moderating role of family supportive supervisor behavior in the relationship between work-family role blurring and taking charge. A moderated mediation model is constructed using boundary theory and work-family border theory as foundational frameworks. The data were collected from 275 professional women in China. Moreover, family supportive supervisor behavior which is a key manifestation of supportive leadership in the modern, boundary-less workplace moderates the relationship between work-family role blurring and job engagement. Additionally, moderated mediation results confirm that a higher level of family supportive supervisor behavior increases professional women’s taking charge level through the indirect effect of work-family role blurring via job engagement. The findings highlight that in an era of pervasive digital connectivity, cultivating family supportive supervisor behaviors is a crucial strategy for management to mitigate role blurring and enhance professional women’s proactive workplace behaviors. This study enriches our understanding of the underlying processes of taking charge by developing a more comprehensive model that integrates the challenges of digital-era work design with the resource-providing function of leadership.

Purpose This study aims to adopt a processual perspective to examine how early career teachers manage job demands and use organisational resources in a learning-intensive environment, exploring how work, learning and engagement manifest in their daily activities. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative, abductive design was used based on 15 semi-structured interviews with early career teachers in a UK Academy Trust. Data were analysed using an iterative thematic approach, combining data-led coding with later-stage theoretical engagement with the job demands–resources (JD–R) framework and workplace-learning perspectives. Findings The analysis identified recurring patterns through which the teachers’ interpreted demands, engaged with organisational cues and reworked the available sources of guidance. Participants consistently understood the demands, and organisational resources were used based on their specific features and their availability. When feedback and organisational signals were limited, teachers engaged in resource substitution, a set of situated practices in which they assembled provisional reference points from alternative guidance sources, including peer interactions, task-related cues and reflections. Originality/value This study contributes a processual account of how demands and resources are used in practice, complementing the established variance-oriented approaches in JD–R literature. By bringing JD–R into dialogue with workplace learning research, this study proposes resource substitution as a contextually situated practice in early career settings.

Smart geospatial technologies are changing the way governments, industries, and societies collect, analyze, and use spatial data to solve complex global challenges. This comprehensive chapter explores the evolution, current state, challenges, emerging trends, real-world applications, and future directions of intelligent geospatial systems, highlighting the transformative impact of integrating artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, the Internet of Things (IoT), unmanned aerial vehicles, light detection and ranging (LiDAR), global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) real-time kinematic (RTK) positioning, and cloud computing technologies into spatial intelligence workflows. New trends such as AI-driven spatial classification, predictive modeling, and automation are signaling a paradigm shift in geospatial intelligence. The geospatial intelligence market, with annual growth rates of over 25% and a projected value exceeding $60 billion, is poised for wide deployment across multiple sectors. Innovations in explainable artificial intelligence, generative AI-based models, and federated learning promise to increase trust, transparency, and privacy in spatial data analytics ( Google Research, 2025) . Additional technological advances include the integration of blockchain to provide decentralized spatial data, quantum and edge computing for ultrafast analytics, the combination of digital twins with building information modeling (BIM) for dynamic urban simulations, and the use of augmented and virtual reality to create interactive geospatial experiences. This chapter highlights these advances through a rich series of real-world case studies. Singapore’s digital twin initiative combines the IoT, BIM, and 3D/4D GIS to optimize resource use, achieving an estimated US$7.5 million in water savings per year while improving air quality monitoring. California’s 2024 wildfire response used AI-driven satellite classification and drone LiDAR maps to reduce emergency response times by 30%. In the Netherlands, precision agriculture projects using drone multispectral imagery with IoT soil sensors increased yields by 10% and reduced fertilizer use by 20%. European infrastructure monitoring demonstrated cost-effective safety improvements through autonomous drone inspection and BIM-GIS integration. In autonomous transportation, Waymo demonstrated a 40% reduction in accident rates by combining GNSS RTK with LiDAR and SLAM technologies. Other applications include monitoring Arctic sea ice for climate modeling, analyzing COVID-19 spatial data to optimize public health interventions in India, and Amsterdam’s smart transportation network, which reduced passenger travel times by 25% and https://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"> CO 2 emissions by 15%. By synthesizing these insights, this chapter presents a holistic framework for researchers, policymakers, urban planners, engineers, data scientists, and industry professionals to understand the changing landscape of smart geospatial technologies. It highlights the importance of responsible adoption, continuous innovation, and strategic collaboration to unleash the transformative potential of spatial intelligence for a smart, safe, and sustainable future.

Expert systems offer an effective alternative for representing specialized knowledge and supporting decision-making through production rules (Russell & Norvig, 2021). This paper presents NetExpert-XAI, an expert system for the explainable diagnosis of faults in local area networks (LANs). The methodology was based on knowledge engineering principles, encompassing knowledge acquisition and representation, the design of a knowledge base, and the implementation of a forward-chaining inference engine using Python and the Experta library (Experta Developers, n.d.). The system integrates a user interface, a fact base, an inference engine, and an explanation module, enabling the generation of justified diagnoses and technical recommendations in accordance with the principles of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (Adadi & Berrada, 2018). The results demonstrate that the prototype effectively replicates the reasoning of network administration specialists and serves as a transparent, scalable tool to support the diagnostic process.

Criticism of media coverage is an essential democratic mechanism to hold journalism accountable, yet it can also foster distrust and perceptions of media bias. This study examines such tensions through the case of the German media discourse on arms deliveries to Ukraine. Using accusations of one-sided reporting as a starting point, we theorize normative expectations of media diversity in war-related policy discourse and empirically assess how leading German news outlets represented competing viewpoints. Drawing on a two-year corpus (2022-2023) from 14 Leitmedien and employing a hierarchical supervised machine-learning approach based on (large) language models, we classify stances and frames to compute standard diversity indices. The results reveal a balanced distribution of supportive and opposing stances, yet a low diversity of argumentative frames. This pattern suggests that German media exhibited a liberal-aggregative model of diversity, emphasizing coexistence of opinions over deliberative engagement with competing interpretations. Despite frequent claims of uniform pro-government bias, our findings indicate that coverage was more heterogeneous than critics claimed. However, they also point to limited argumentative depth and a tendency to reproduce existing political logics. We discuss the methodological and normative challenges of quantifying diversity, particularly under conditions of war and uncertainty, and argue that criticism of media bias often reflects broader transformations in the perception of journalistic diversity.

Abstract Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) faces a hard constraint in public-facing nutri-tion QA: answers must be faithful to official sources. Yet Chinese official nutrition data lacks an auditable evaluation benchmark —numeric faithfulness, refusal bound-aries, and hallucination suppression remain unquantified. We present NutriQA, a traceable RAG question-answering benchmark on official Chinese nutrition data: 200 items in a four-category taxonomy (composition 60 / guideline 50 / special 50 / re-fusal 40), a three-level gold-provenance system (official food-composition values, ver-batim guideline excerpts, gold-free refusal items), and fully auditable deterministic judgment rules (numeric ±1 tolerance + key-point coverage + fabrication detection). Full-scale experiments on three commercial models (qwen-plus, deepseek-chat, glm-5.3-flash) show: (1) hybrid retrieval (BM25 character-bigram + vector RRF, top_k=8) achieves a 160/160 hit rate, with retrieval method choice outweighing chunking gran-ularity; (2) retrieval optimization lifts RAG gain from ~0.15–0.17 to 0.20–0.225, de-coupling retrieval hit from the generator; (3) a novel boundary subclass (out-of-KB foods × numeric baits) quantifies 100% numeric fabrication by bare LLMs over out-of-KB objects with mutually exclusive cross-model intervals (3–4× apart), which RAG compresses to ~0–2.5% via“retrieved-not-covered → refuse”; (4) deterministic rules agree with human annotation at 0.949, outperforming a generic LLM judge at 0.846. Data, code, and full evidence are pinned at git tag v1.0.0 for independent verification and reproduction.

This chapter examines how AI is transforming occupational health and disease surveillance by strengthening disease detection, exposure assessment, predictive analytics, and integrated occupational health management. Building upon the ESH Management System and PRIM governance framework introduced in earlier chapters, it demonstrates how AI enables organizations to move beyond traditional, reactive surveillance toward continuous, data-driven prevention of occupational illness and disease. This chapter explores the three primary components of occupational surveillance – health surveillance, hazard surveillance, and sentinel surveillance – and illustrates how each contributes to the early identification of workplace hazards, disease trends, and emerging occupational health risks. It examines the application of machine learning, predictive analytics, wearable technologies, environmental monitoring systems, and decision-support tools to improve disease detection, real-time exposure monitoring, resource prioritization, and occupational health response. This chapter also explores the relationship between environmental conditions and disease patterns, demonstrating how environmental factors, workplace exposures, and public health surveillance influence occupational disease prevention and long-term worker health. Finally, it presents an integrated approach to predictive occupational health analysis by combining environmental monitoring, safety performance data, and occupational health information into unified analytical systems capable of identifying emerging risks before adverse health outcomes occur. Throughout this chapter, AI is presented as a decision-support technology that complements occupational health professionals while emphasizing responsible governance, interdisciplinary collaboration, data quality, and ethical implementation. Collectively, these capabilities strengthen occupational disease surveillance, improve worker protection, enhance regulatory compliance, and support more proactive, evidence-based occupational health management within the modern ESH Management System.

documents.abstract: This chapter examines how AI is transforming occupational health monitoring by enhancing medical surveillance, worker health assessment, wearable technologies, and remote healthcare capabilities within ESH Management Systems. Building upon the PRIM governance framework introduced in earlier chapters, this chapter demonstrates how AI enables organizations to transition from periodic, reactive health assessments to continuous, proactive monitoring of worker well-being. It explores the integration of machine learning, biometric sensors, wearable technologies, IoT devices, and predictive analytics to strengthen hazard detection, health surveillance, early intervention, and occupational risk management. This chapter examines the use of wearable technologies to monitor physiological and environmental indicators – including heart rate, body temperature, fatigue, stress, movement, and hazardous exposures – providing real-time insights ^gthat improve worker protection and operational decision-making. AI-driven stress and fatigue detection are presented as critical capabilities for identifying early warning signs that may impair cognitive performance, increase accident risk, or reduce productivity, enabling timely interventions before adverse events occur. This chapter also explores remote health diagnostics and telemedicine, demonstrating how AI, connected health technologies, and mobile health platforms support continuous health monitoring, clinical decision support, and personalized care beyond traditional healthcare settings. Throughout this chapter, AI is presented as a decision-support technology that complements occupational health professionals while emphasizing the importance of privacy, transparency, ethical governance, and worker-centered implementation. Collectively, these technologies strengthen occupational health programs by improving worker well-being, regulatory compliance, organizational resilience, and the overall effectiveness of modern Occupational Health Management Systems.

documents.abstract: Academic emergency departments (EDs) host off-service residents (OSRs) from various specialties. While OSRs contribute meaningfully to patient care, they often face unique challenges during their ED rotations, including limited preparation, heightened stress, and unmet personal expectations. Despite a standardized curriculum endorsed by the American College of Emergency Physicians, guidance on how to foster meaningful educational experiences for OSRs remains sparse. This perspective offers a structured approach grounded in self-determination theory (SDT), which emphasizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness as essential to intrinsic motivation and effective learning. By aligning educational strategies with SDT principles, emergency medicine educators can enhance engagement, support learner development, and create lasting interprofessional collaboration. Ultimately, this learner-centered approach not only enriches the OSR experience but also strengthens the role of the ED as a dynamic, inclusive learning environment for all trainees.

Engagement in virtual learning is critical to participant satisfaction, performance, and adherence, particularly in domains such as online education and virtual rehabilitation, where interactive communication is essential for success. However, accurately measuring engagement in virtual group settings remains a significant challenge. There is growing interest in leveraging artificial intelligence for large-scale, real-world, and automated engagement recognition. Although engagement has been widely studied among younger populations in academic contexts, research methods and datasets focused on older adults in virtual and telehealth learning environments remain limited. Existing approaches often overlook the contextual relevance of learning materials and the longitudinal dynamics of engagement across sessions. This paper presents OPEN (Older adult Patient ENgagement), a novel dataset created to support the development of artificial intelligence models for engagement recognition. The dataset was collected from eleven older adults participating in virtual group learning sessions over six weeks as part of their cardiac rehabilitation programs, yielding over 35 hours of data, which represents the largest dataset of its kind. While raw video is withheld to protect privacy, the publicly released data include facial, hand, and body joint landmarks, as well as behavioral and affective features extracted from video. Observational annotations comprise second-level binary engagement states, emotional and behavioral labels, and context-type details, such as whether the instructor addressed the group or an individual. Multiple versions of the dataset were generated using sample lengths of 5, 10, and 30 seconds, as well as variable-length segments. To demonstrate its utility, various machine learning and deep learning models were trained on the annotated data, achieving engagement recognition accuracy as high as 81%. OPEN provides a scalable foundation not only for advancing personalized, artificial intelligence-driven engagement recognition in aging populations but also for contributing to broader engagement recognition research.

This study investigates operational drivers of fuel performance in maritime transport using 22 months of high-resolution sensor data from two Ro-Ro sister vessels. A hybrid benchmark model is developed to derive a speed-and draught-independent performance indicator, enabling consistent evaluation of efficiency and environmental impact. Results show that fuel performance is primarily governed by physical operating conditions, while hull condition and human factors are associated with variability in observed performance. Hull degradation leads to efficiency losses through increased resistance and associated operational responses, with implications for fuel consumption and emissions. Variability related to captains and crews are explained by how operating conditions are selected and managed rather than by intrinsic performance differences. A machine learning-based decision support pilot showed a 1.9 percentage-point improvement in fuel performance and reduced variability across operators. Overall, the findings demonstrate how maintenance, operational decisions, and data-driven tools can enhance transport efficiency and support maritime decarbonisation.
