documents.abstract: This paper examines whether talent attraction policies promote firm-level artificial intelligence (AI) intensity. Using panel data on Chinese listed firms from 2005 to 2023, we exploit the staggered adoption of city-level talent attraction policies and estimate a staggered difference-in-differences model. We find that these policies significantly increase AI intensity among firms located in treated cities. Mechanism analysis shows that these policies increase the accumulation of highly educated employees in local firms. Additional evidence on R&D and digital asset investment is consistent with the capital–skill complementarity channel. We also find that urban digital infrastructure strengthens the policy effect. Moreover, analysis by keyword category shows increases in references to AI applications and complementary digital activities in firms’ annual reports. Further analysis shows that the policy effects are stronger in higher-tier and wealthier cities. These findings provide firm-level causal evidence on the role of human capital in AI development and offer policy implications for designing talent policies that support the diffusion of AI technologies.

Objective To determine how cognitive fatigue (CF) affects subjective experience and reaction time (RT) performance across tasks with different processing demands (simple, go/no-go, choice), and whether these effects depend on the type of fatigue-inducing mental work. Background CF is a psychobiological state of subjective exhaustion from mental effort that can compromise workplace productivity and safety. Although slowed RT is an often-observed consequence of CF, it is unclear how this compares across RT paradigms and fatigue-inducing tasks. Method Using a remotely administered experiment, 402 participants completed a 60-minute CF (Math-Memory, Stroop, Time Load Dual-Back) or control (documentary) intervention. Subjective ratings (mental fatigue, motivation) and RT performance (simple, go/no-go, choice) were assessed pre- and post-intervention. Results Relative to control, all CF tasks increased subjective fatigue ( p < .001), while motivation declined following Dual-Back and Stroop ( p ≤ .030) but not Math-Memory. Simple and choice RT slowed significantly following all CF interventions vs control ( p < .010), with the greatest choice RT slowing after Stroop ( p ≤ .032). Only Stroop produced significant go/no-go RT slowing ( p = .004). Conclusion Subjective fatigue and simple RT were broadly sensitive to CF, indicating general psychomotor slowing. Conversely, motivation and higher-complexity RT measures showed task-specific effects, perhaps reflecting overlap between fatigue-inducing and RT task demands. Application Task type is important when considering RT as a fatigue assessment tool. These findings support multidimensional (subjective and RT) CF assessments and indicate that simple RT may be effective for rapid, broad fatigue monitoring, whereas complex RT metrics may be useful when exploring task-specific executive processing effects.

Abstract Digital transformation is reshaping teaching and learning worldwide, yet its benefits remain unevenly distributed and the competences it demands of educators are still contested. This article asks how different educational stakeholders conceptualise the competences required for effective digitalisation of teaching and learning, and what they identify as the principal obstacles to it. The study forms part of an international Erasmus+ Teacher Academy project using a shared interview protocol across partner countries; this article reports the Latvian data. Thirty-two participants - pre-service teachers, in-service teachers and educational leaders, took part in semi-structured interviews, analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Four findings stand out. First, the competences participants named varied systematically with their position in the system: pre-service teachers emphasised operational skills, in-service teachers pedagogical integration, and leaders strategic change management; strikingly few future-oriented competences were technological. Second, language operated as a double constraint, with English proficiency governing access to tools and professional learning while a scarcity of high-quality Latvian-language resources limited classroom use. Third, artificial intelligence was experienced primarily as a challenge to assessment rather than to teaching. Fourth, barriers internal to teachers fear of error and a perceived generational divide, persisted even in well-resourced schools, and change was carried largely by early-adopting colleagues rather than institutional mandate. Together these findings indicate that investment in equipment alone will not deliver digital transformation, and that professional development, resource policy and assessment design need to be addressed as a single problem rather than three separate ones.

Introduction The rapid expansion of generative AI has intensified scholarly and policy debate over its role in higher education, yet university teachers’ attitudes towards its integration remain complex and context-dependent. This study explores how university teachers perceive, experience, and respond to AI integration in their teaching. Guided primarily by the three-component attitude model and informed by the technology acceptance model and the theory of planned behaviour, the study examines cognitive appraisals, affective responses, behavioural intentions, and perceived support needs. Methods The study draws on semi-structured interviews with 14 university teachers from four higher education institutions in China. The interview data were analysed using codebook-informed thematic analysis combining deductive and inductive coding. Results The findings indicate that teachers generally perceive AI as a supportive rather than substitutive educational tool, valuing it for improving efficiency, supporting lesson preparation, and enriching pedagogical design. Emotional responses varied from enthusiasm and a sense of accomplishment to caution, neutrality, and, in some cases, declining satisfaction. Across the interviews, teachers’ primary concerns centred less on their own replacement than on the perceived risks of inappropriate AI use for students’ independent thinking, reasoning, originality, and authentic understanding. Teachers’ intentions to adopt AI were therefore conditional and bounded, shaped by pedagogical purpose, disciplinary context, student readiness, and the need to maintain teacher control. Teachers also emphasised that sustainable AI integration requires more than general encouragement, calling instead for AI literacy development, discipline-sensitive support, specialised tools, and enabling institutional infrastructure. Discussion Overall, these findings extend contextual understandings of teachers’ AI acceptance by showing how adoption intentions are pedagogically negotiated and highlight the importance of supporting professional judgement and students’ independent thinking in higher education.

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new opportunities for instructional innovation, yet the psychological mechanisms underlying teachers’ intentions to adopt it remain unclear. Intrinsic motivation is an important internal factor shaping teachers’ intentions to use GenAI and is closely linked to the satisfaction of their basic psychological needs. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), this study develops and tests a theoretical framework linking teachers’ basic psychological need satisfaction to their intention to use GenAI through intrinsic motivation and engagement in professional development. Such engagement may foster innovation in GenAI-supported teaching practices. Methods Survey data were collected from 146 teachers participating in a GenAI learning program. Structural equation modeling was used to examine the hypothesized relationships among basic psychological need satisfaction, intrinsic motivation, engagement in professional development, and intention to use GenAI. Results Perceived competence in using GenAI was significantly and positively associated with intrinsic motivation, whereas perceived autonomy and relatedness were not significantly associated with intrinsic motivation. Engagement in professional development mediated the relationship between intrinsic motivation and intention to use GenAI. Discussion These findings provide a nuanced understanding of the psychological mechanisms underlying teachers’ intentions to adopt GenAI, highlighting the roles of perceived competence, intrinsic motivation, and engagement in professional development. They also offer practical implications for supporting the integration of GenAI into teaching.

Management educators face the urgent task of moving students beyond passive consumption to strategic, critical use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). The goal of this article is to provide a structured framework that transforms GenAI into a tool for cognitive partnership. We present a complete guide for a semester-long, multi-session assignment, designed for undergraduate management education. The assignment’s purpose is to deepen conceptual understanding through experiential learning that combines concept mapping with the critical, comparative use of multiple GenAI tools. Students research a company, build iterative visual knowledge structures, use artificial intelligence (AI) to challenge assumptions, and engage in reflective critical thinking. The teaching focus is on fostering AI literacy and strategic reasoning. This assignment provides instructors with a pedagogically sound method to leverage emerging technologies for active, deep learning in business courses.

This paper investigates the challenge posed by Large Language Models (LLMs) to teaching and learning how to write at the post-secondary level, situating LLMs as a form of automation affecting both the labour of educators and the labour-markets our students will enter on graduation. The paper argues that the arrival of the chatbot should spur universities to refocus on process-oriented approaches to writing instruction, which foreground the cognitive labour of writing as a practice of thinking. Understanding what writing is – as a practice rather than a product – is critical to understanding the role we should play as university teachers in relation to LLMs as a form of automation that will displace some, but not all, of the capacities that university-level writing practices are meant to cultivate.

Citation intent classification identifies the underlying functions of scholarly citations and provides semantic information beyond citation counts. However, existing methods pay limited attention to temporal information in citation relationships and are often constrained by the scarcity of high-quality annotated data. To address these challenges, we propose TempCL-Cite, a temporal-aware contrastive learning framework that jointly exploits publication time gaps and large language model (LLM)-generated positive examples. TempCL-Cite encodes the publication time gap and fuses it with textual representations, while using temporal-gap differences together with label differences to guide negative sampling. In addition, a prompt-based LLM generates paraphrases of citation contexts conditioned on their intent labels, providing additional positive views for contrastive learning. The LLM is used only for offline data augmentation and is not required during inference. Experiments on three benchmark datasets show that TempCL-Cite achieves the highest mean Accuracy and Macro-F1 among the compared methods. Ablation results indicate that temporal modeling and contrastive learning contribute to performance in the evaluated settings. Furthermore, temporal-gap-constrained negative sampling outperforms both label-only selection and matched-number random sampling on all three datasets. Comparisons with same-label positives and dropout views show that the proposed LLM-based positive construction strategy achieves the highest mean scores among the evaluated alternatives. BERTScore results indicate strong semantic similarity between the generated and original citation contexts.

Malware detection remains a critical challenge in computer science and cybersecurity due to the continuous evolution of malicious software, concept drift, and the declining generalization capability of machine learning models over time. This study investigates the temporal performance of hybrid artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models for static malware detection using the EMBER dataset. A quantitative experimental design is employed to compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM, and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) classifiers with a hybrid ensemble approach. The methodology incorporates feature preprocessing, chronological data partitioning, supervised model training, and temporal performance evaluation using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). Comparative analysis examined differences in classification performance and temporal degradation across the evaluated models. Confusion-matrix analysis and false-negative rates were also considered to assess classification reliability and identify potential detection errors. The hybrid framework combined tree-based learning and neural network predictions to investigate classification performance and detection consistency across temporally distinct malware samples. The significance of this research lies in addressing the limitations of conventional random-split evaluation and providing a more realistic framework for assessing the temporal generalization of intelligent malware detection systems. The findings are intended to inform the development of adaptive, scalable, and robust cybersecurity solutions capable of responding to evolving malware threats.

Task-based language teaching (TBLT) is increasingly advocated in a range of contexts across the globe as an effective learner-centred and experiential alternative to more traditional teacher-led and instructivist approaches. However, its implementation in classrooms has not always been straightforward. In practice, teachers often struggle not only with understanding what a task is for the purposes of TBLT but also with how tasks fit into the broader learner-centred and experiential pedagogical approach that informs TBLT. Additionally, time constraints and workload pressures have been identified as significant barriers to effective TBLT implementation. In the context of teacher education, this paper considers to what extent ChatGPT as an open access generative artificial intelligence application can support TESOL practitioners with not only generating tasks that are appropriately aligned to TBLT theory but also streamlining the lesson and resource planning and preparation process. The present study investigated what 39 participants in a dedicated postgraduate course focused on TBLT thought of using ChatGPT to design a task, with associated pre-task and post-task activities, for potential classroom use. It draws on data from individual reflective presentations given at the end of the course. Six themes were constructed from a reflexive thematic analysis – three benefits and three limitations of using ChatGPT for task creation purposes. In light of perceived advantages and disadvantages, participants saw using ChatGPT for task generation as a ‘yes … but’ proposition. The findings raise key issues for teachers and teacher educators to be mindful of when using tools like ChatGPT to design tasks.

Proposals for governing artificial intelligence (AI) are often judged by completeness: how much risk they cover before deployment. This paper argues that the alignment problem is also a rate problem. Frontier AI capability, institutional governance capacity, and the supply of high-quality training data change at different rates. Waiting for complete governance before acting therefore carries its own risk, because the gap between capability and governance capacity can widen during the delay. The paper proposes the Nash-Pareto Hybrid Equilibrium (NPHE) as a deliberately incomplete and revisable governance counterweight. NPHE addresses one bounded governance function: real-time regulation of an AI system’s behavioral latitude against a human-ratified setpoint. A threat-weighting function blends defensive and cooperative posture vectors. A critical-integrity override prevents a severe single-axis failure from being averaged away. A bounded discrete proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller adjusts the blend. The principal contribution is a computable specification of the alignment-error term that the controller requires, with an explicit account of which components are specified, unbuilt, or uncalibrated. NPHE is a conceptual architecture and research agenda, not a validated controller. The estimator, setpoint, and intervention-response dynamics remain unbuilt or unidentified. The controller gains are provisional, and the paper claims no stability proof.

documents.abstract: Background and Objective: Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in medicine is rapidly expanding, including ambient AI (AAI), which converts clinician-patient conversations into documentation. Despite growing use among practicing physicians, little is known about student access to AAI or barriers to implementation during medical student clerkships.Methods: We surveyed 174 family medicine clerkship directors (CDs) through the Council of Academic Family Medicine Educational Research Alliance network regarding AAI availability, permissibility, and opinions on student use. We analyzed responses using descriptive statistics and Fisher’s exact tests.Results: Ninety-four CDs responded to AAI-related questions. Student AAI use was permitted for only 3% of core family medicine clerkships. CDs cited missing technology (38.3%) or institutional restrictions (42.5%) as barriers. Opinions on student use were divided: 42.6% opposed any use, 41.5% supported some use, and 16% were unsure. Among those who opposed use, major concerns included potential negative effects on clinical reasoning (82.5%) and communication skills (85%). Supporters of student use were significantly more likely to believe AI will improve training and become commonplace in students’ careers than those who did not support student use of AAI (P<0.0001).Conclusions: Access to AAI for medical students during core family medicine clerkships is rare, and CDs expressed substantial concerns regarding its impact on clinical reasoning and communication skills. Given the expeditious integration of AI into clinical practice, medical educators must be prepared to teach with technology, proactively design curricula that assume AAI availability, and consider modalities in addition to clinical documentation to assess student clinical reasoning.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background and aims: With the rapid development of conversational artificial intelligence (CAI), problematic use of conversational AI (PUCAI) among adolescents has attracted increasing attention. However, the underlying psychological factors associated with PUCAI remain unclear. Guided by the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model, this study explored the associations between interpersonal alienation, perceived anthropomorphism, AI attachment, and PUCAI. Methods: Data were collected from 1,124 Chinese high school students (516 males, 608 females; Mage = 16.59). Serial mediation analysis and network analysis were conducted. Results: Interpersonal alienation was positively associated with PUCAI. It also had indirect associations through both parallel and serial mediation involving perceived anthropomorphism and AI attachment. Network analysis further revealed that perceived anthropomorphism exhibited the highest bridge expected influence, and emotional trust showed the highest centrality. Conclusion: These findings suggest that adolescent PUCAI is associated not only with general psychological risk factors but also with social-cognitive perceptions and emotional bonding experiences during human-AI interactions. This study provides a novel perspective for understanding problematic use behaviors in emerging human-AI interaction contexts and offers implications for future risk assessment and research on healthy AI use.

This study investigates the effect of organizational artificial intelligence (AI) absorptive capacity on employees’ perceptions of the smart work environment and how these perceptions influence their digital innovative behavior in the telecommunications industry, with Digital Transformational Leadership as a moderating variable. In this study, two important theoretical perspectives were utilized: Absorptive Capacity Theory, which highlights how organizations acquire, assimilate, and apply their knowledge related to AI, and Socio-Technical Systems Theory, which addresses the connection between technology and the social aspect of the working environment. A quantitative research design was used through partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The data were gathered from 279 respondents working in the telecommunication industry in Jordan. These respondents worked for internet service providers, network operators, and mobile network operators. The findings show that organizational AI absorptive capacity has a strong positive effect on Smart Work Environment Perception (β = 0.742), which in turn enhances Digital Innovative Behavior (β = 0.681). Smart Work Environment Perception partially mediates the relationship between AI absorptive capacity and Digital Innovative Behavior (indirect effect β = 0.506), while Digital Transformational Leadership positively moderates the relationship between AI absorptive capacity and the smart work environment (β = 0.276) and between the smart work environment and Digital Innovative Behavior (β = 0.241). The current research adds value to the literature surrounding AI adoption within organizations by examining how technical capabilities and organizational leadership help foster Digital Innovative Behavior in the telecommunications industry.

High school biology learning is often hindered by abstract concepts and cognitive overload, leading to low student motivation. Although generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and gamification show instructional potential, their combined motivational effects remain underexplored. Grounded in the ARCS model, this study examined the impact of integrating ChatGPT-based GenAI and gamification on students’ Attention, Relevance, Confidence, and Satisfaction. A longitudinal quasi-experimental repeated measures design was conducted with 52 high school biology students over eight weeks. Motivation was measured at four time points using a validated ARCS questionnaire and analyzed with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results showed significant improvements across all ARCS dimensions from pre- to post-intervention (p < .001). Attention and relevance increased steadily, confidence improved in later stages, and satisfaction rose overall. Reported challenges included limited personalized AI feedback, competition-induced anxiety associated with leaderboard-based competition, and increased cognitive load resulting from complex AI-generated content. The findings indicate that GenAI-supported gamification can enhance motivation in biology learning when supported by careful pedagogical design.

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes an imperative survival strategy for modern enterprises, numerous organizations continue to face implementation failures stemming from employees’ psychological resistance. To address the scarcity of empirical research regarding the practical and psychological acceptance of AI in workflows, this study investigates the structural relationships between technological maturity and users’ cognitive adoption. Grounded in an integrated framework utilizing the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), this research conceptualizes the “AI Environment Factor” as a higher-order construct comprising four foundational sub-dimensions: AI System Quality, AI Information Quality, AI Data Quality, and AI Infrastructure. A quantitative survey was administered to 189 corporate practitioners who have utilized enterprise-wide AI systems for at least one year, and the empirical data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The analytical results indicate that the AI Environment Factor exerts a statistically significant positive effect on both Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness. Furthermore, Perceived Ease of Use was found to positively influence Perceived Usefulness. Ultimately, both Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness are significantly associated with the employees’ continuous AI Intention to Use. These findings theoretically contribute to the literature by providing a measurable structural model for the continuance intention phase of organizational AI adoption. Practically, this study offers actionable guidelines for corporate executives, emphasizing that securing rigorous data accuracy and a stable system infrastructure is indispensable for mitigating cognitive load, fostering innovative corporate cultures, and maximizing the efficacy of AI utilization.

documents.abstract: Surgery is increasingly recognized as a complex, longitudinal therapeutic process spanning preoperative preparation, anesthesia, intraoperative care, and postoperative recovery rather than an isolated operating room event. Because this continuum is highly medication-intensive and subject to challenges like polypharmacy, rapid drug administration, physiological instability, multiple transitions of care, and communication failures, the perioperative environment carries a high risk for preventable medication errors. This review explores the evolving role of the clinical pharmacist, transitioning from a passive dispenser to an active, multidisciplinary collaborator throughout the surgical pathway. In the preoperative phase, clinical pharmacists improve patient safety by constructing a best possible medication history, clarifying continuation or cessation plans for high-risk home therapies (such as anticoagulants and antidiabetics), and delivering patient education to reduce morning-of-surgery non-adherence. In the intraoperative phase, they support anesthesia providers through system-level and case-level interventions, including the standardization of medication trays and labeling, antimicrobial prophylaxis stewardship, and multimodal analgesic design. Postoperatively, pharmacists collaborate with anesthesiologists to optimize acute pain management, support opioid stewardship, manage thromboembolism prophylaxis, and coordinate comprehensive discharge reconciliation to prevent drug duplication or omission. Collaborative models-such as joint acute pain services and pre-anesthesia consultations-render medication reviews clinically actionable and significantly enhance therapy optimization. Although challenges like staffing constraints, training gaps, and inconsistent clinical integration persist, the future of perioperative pharmacy lies in proactive, technology-enabled care incorporating clinical decision support, barcode administration, and artificial intelligence to solidify clinical pharmacists as core contributors to surgical patient safety.

Against digital education background, generative AI has become common writing assistance for undergraduates. Existing studies mainly focus on second-language writing and ignore stratified comparisons across learners, while the dual effects of AI on academic writing self-efficacy remain understudied. Based on self-efficacy theory, this paper distributes questionnaires and divides respondents into three proficiency groups by CET-4 scores. Descriptive statistics, group difference tests and correlation analysis are adopted for empirical analysis. The results reveal prevalent AI over-dependence despite its polishing functions. Participants’ writing self-efficacy stays at medium-upper level yet hampered by writing anxiety. AI delivers short-term confidence promotion but impairs independent writing competence in the long run, with stronger influences on low-proficiency students. This stratified dual-path framework offers empirical references for standardized AI application in university writing teaching.

Subject of Research. This study focuses on the digital banking landscape and the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in private banking and wealth management in Switzerland. More specifically, it examines how technological innovations – ranging from process automation and generative AI to advanced data analytics – alter the operational dynamics, customer relations, and structural competitiveness of Swiss private banks in the context of shifting client expectations and rigorous regulatory environments. Methodology. The research employs a qualitative analytical research design that uses triangulation of secondary evidence. It systematically integrates and cross-checks academic literature on digital finance, fintech adoption and robo-advisory trust, alongside empirical data, regulatory frameworks and market insights from reputable Swiss and international organisations. The primary data sources analysed were supervisory guides from the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA), reports from the Swiss Bankers Association, digital maturity benchmarks from Deloitte Switzerland and private banking market profitability assessments from KPMG and PwC Switzerland. Purpose. The main objective of this paper is to provide a comprehensive assessment of the impact of digital transformation and the deployment of AI on the traditional Swiss private banking model. By analysing seven key dimensions – technological progress, customer expectations, process optimization, data analytics, risk and security, regulation/compliance, and market trajectories – the study aims to clarify the economic mechanisms driving digital adaptation, identify the structural barriers preventing rapid technology adoption, and evaluate the strategic options available to Swiss banks facing intense global competition and margin compression. Findings and Conclusion. The study reveals a significant discrepancy between Switzerland's position as a global leader in asset management, with CHF 9.3 trillion under management, and its digital banking maturity score of 39 out of 60. Although private banking clients continue to establish relationships based on traditional factors such as reputation, trust and personal referrals, they are also demanding friction-free digital execution, personalised dashboards and virtual investment simulations. AI has been proven to have high economic value when acting as a productivity layer centred around advisors, optimising processes such as client onboarding, document extraction, compliance screening and portfolio monitoring. However, it is not as effective when acting as an autonomous replacement for human relationship managers. Ultimately, the integration of digital banking and AI is causing a clear market polarisation. Large-scale institutions are successfully absorbing the substantial fixed costs associated with technology, data governance and regulatory compliance under the frameworks of FINMA and the European Union (such as DORA and the EU AI Act). Conversely, smaller Swiss private banks are under severe pressure to increase their profitability and consolidate, unless they adopt highly focused niche advisory models. The paper therefore concludes that urgent regulatory attention and strategic repositioning are necessary to preserve the overall image and international attractiveness of the Swiss private banking ecosystem.

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and Claude into everyday work practices has created a new and poorly governed channel through which organizational data can leave the enterprise. This review synthesized theoretical, empirical, and practitioner literature on the relationship between employees' integration of GenAI tools and organizational data exposure risks, situating that relationship within the broader context of organizational data security posture. The review is organized around four themes, the extent, drivers, and patterns of employee GenAI integration in the workplace, the phenomenon of "Shadow AI" and "Bring Your Own AI" (BYOAI), the mechanisms through which GenAI use generates data exposure, leakage, and compliance risks, and the role of data security posture encompassing governance frameworks, visibility, policy, and employee security behavior in moderating those risks. Literature from developed economies dominates the field, while evidence from Uganda and the wider Sub-Saharan African context remains scarce. The review identifies key theoretical anchors (the Technology Acceptance Model, Protection Motivation Theory, and information security governance perspectives), synthesized documented incidents such as the Samsung ChatGPT data leak, and highlights empirical survey evidence showing widespread unsanctioned use of GenAI by employees. It concludes by delineating conceptual and empirical gaps particularly the absence of studies that jointly model GenAI integration, data exposure risk, and data security posture in developing country organizational settings and proposes a conceptual framework to guide future research in Ugandan organizations.

Against the backdrop of the digital economy, the deep integration of artificial intelligence and Internet of Things technologies has driven the rapid adoption of smart home appliances, providing new pathways for energy conservation, emissions reduction, and sustainable consumption in households. However, the psychological mechanisms underlying the transformation of smart home appliance technology perceptions into sustainable consumption behaviors—particularly the serial mediating roles of perceived value and perceived consumer effectiveness—remain to be thoroughly investigated. Based on the SOR theory, a research model was constructed with perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use as stimulus variables, perceived value and perceived consumer effectiveness as organism variables, and sustainable consumption behavior as the response variable. Empirical analysis was conducted using SmartPLS based on 508 valid questionnaires. The results indicate that the model exhibits good explanatory power (R2 = 50.4%), with significant positive relationships among all variables. Among these, perceived usefulness has a positive association with perceived value; perceived value is significantly associated with perceived consumer effectiveness; and perceived consumer effectiveness has a significant direct association with sustainable consumption behavior. Furthermore, perceived value and perceived consumer effectiveness play significant mediating and serial mediating roles. This study reveals the psychological transmission mechanism through which the perceived technology of smart home appliances influences sustainable consumption behavior, expands the application of SOR theory, and provides a theoretical basis and practical guidance for smart home appliance companies to formulate green marketing strategies oriented toward value enhancement and efficacy strengthening.

Abstract Academic libraries are currently undergoing fundamental change. Digitisation, open access, research data management, artificial intelligence, changing learning and research practices, and the transformation of the publishing system are broadening their remit whilst simultaneously raising users’ expectations of them. In international professional discourse, this development is often described as a transition from a collection-centred library to one that is more service- and workflow-oriented. (Dempsey and Malpas 2018; Pinfield, Cox and Rutter 2017; Lavoie and Bryant 2026) This brings with it new opportunities. Libraries can develop new services, align themselves more closely with research and learning processes, and expand their role as an infrastructure for academic communication. At the same time, an institutional tension is emerging. Library services are increasingly breaking down into individual services, some of which could also be provided by other organisational units. This makes the question of what enables the library to remain recognisable as a library all the more pressing. This article proposes framing this question using the concept of the ‘functional identity continuum’. This does not imply a static adherence to traditional forms, but rather an interconnection between collection, selection, cataloguing, contextualisation, access, space, preservation, outreach and institutional responsibility. From this perspective, the library of the future remains a plausible institutional form only if it sustainably integrates new services and anchors them to a core library function.

documents.abstract: Abstract Despite the increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education, the psychological mechanisms linking learners’ technological dispositions and emotional experiences to perceived learning effectiveness remain undertheorized and empirically underexplored. This study examined whether self-efficacy served as a statistical mediator in the relationships of technophilia and positive emotional experience with perceived learning effectiveness in AI-supported EFL education. A cross-sectional survey was conducted involving 234 students enrolled in English-language courses at a private college of health sciences. Adapted multi-item scales on technophilia, positive emotional experience, self-efficacy, and perceived learning effectiveness were administered. Structural equation modeling with bootstrapping (5000 resamples) was used to examine direct and indirect associations. Self-efficacy demonstrated the strongest direct association with perceived learning effectiveness (β = 0.375, p = 0.001). Positive emotional experience was strongly associated with self-efficacy (β = 0.624, p < 0.001), and its indirect association with perceived learning effectiveness through self-efficacy was significant (β = 0.234, 95% CI [0.128, 0.351]). Technophilia was also positively associated with self-efficacy (β = 0.307, p = 0.002), and its indirect association with perceived learning effectiveness through self-efficacy was significant. The findings were consistent with self-efficacy partially mediating both relationships. These findings suggest that learners’ confidence in managing AI-supported tasks plays an important role in linking affective dispositions to perceived effectiveness appraisals. The study contributes to computer-assisted language learning (CALL) research by clarifying how positive orientation toward AI-supported technologies, emotional experience, and efficacy beliefs jointly relate to learners’ perceptions of effective AI-supported language learning. Pedagogically, the findings suggest that progressively scaffolded practice and mastery-oriented AI tasks may strengthen self-efficacy and improve learners’ perceived effectiveness in AI-supported EFL environments.

documents.abstract: This chapter traces the evolution of artificial intelligence, from its foundational concepts and early research to modern machine learning, neural networks, and large-scale AI systems. It introduces key AI learning approaches and examines the parallel evolution of SAP, from its early enterprise systems through SAP HANA and SAP S/4HANA to the AI-powered Intelligent Enterprise.

documents.abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is one of the most biologically heterogeneous disorders in reproductive endocrinology, extending far beyond the classical features of hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology. Although substantial progress has been made in defining the endocrine, metabolic, genetic, epigenetic, and inflammatory mechanisms associated with PCOS, these processes have largely been investigated independently, and their contribution to the marked clinical and biological heterogeneity of the disorder remains incompletely understood. Recent advances in cellular-resolution biology, including single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomics, spatial omics, and multimodal molecular profiling, together with computational systems biology, enable increasingly detailed characterization of cellular states, spatial organization, and molecular relationships within the ovarian-follicular environment. In this Review, we use the ovarian cellular ecosystem as an operational systems framework to test whether PCOS-associated abnormalities observed in individual ovarian and follicular compartments form reproducible higher-order patterns of multicellular organization. The framework is organized across five measurable domains: cellular composition and states, intercellular signaling relationships, spatial niche organization, cross-compartment molecular coupling, and systemic-ovarian coupling. Current direct human cellular-resolution evidence remains sparse and compartment-specific. Available studies support altered molecular and cellular states within selected ovarian and follicular compartments more strongly than coordinated, spatially organized, or progressive ecosystem-wide remodeling. We critically evaluate how cellular-resolution, spatial, multi-omics, computational and artificial intelligence approaches can be used to test these ecosystem-level hypotheses, explicitly distinguishing direct measurement from computational inference and identifying the validation required for functional or causal interpretation. Finally, we discuss the translational implications of this framework for biologically informed patient stratification, ecosystem-derived biomarker discovery, mechanism-informed therapeutic development, and precision reproductive endocrinology. By integrating current evidence within a falsifiable framework, this Review defines measurable features and validation criteria for testing ovarian ecosystem organization in PCOS and identifies the critical evidence gaps that future cellular-resolution, spatial, and multi-omic studies must address. This provides a practical roadmap for determining whether reproducible ovarian ecosystem states can improve biological stratification, biomarker discovery, or therapeutic target identification beyond compartment-specific abnormalities and established systemic and clinical determinants.

The Metacognitive Creative Destruction (MCD) model approaches educational innovation as a perpetual spiral process. Contradiction (accumulated cognitive conflicts that resist interpretation), activates Metacognitive Capacity, enabling Destructive Unlearning Propensity, the conscious abandonment of outdated mental schemas, which in turn enables Creative Reconstruction Ability, and ultimately, new knowledge. In the model’s empirical validation with 1,498 teachers, a critical finding emerged: AI Augmentation Intensity (AIA) predicted Metacognitive Capacity (MC) and Creative Reconstruction Ability (CRA), but not Destructive Unlearning Propensity (DUP).This article argues that this finding is not accidental, but reflects an inherent weakness of modern AI systems, and more specifically, the tendency toward AI Sycophancy. Models trained with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) tend to avoid disagreements and be likable to the user, preventing the individual from experiencing cognitive conflicts, perpetuating their already formed beliefs at the expense of scientific accuracy.Therefore, in an environment of “algorithmic flattery”, the necessary contradictions that trigger unlearning are not produced. Based on the MCD model, it is concluded that the absence of unlearning, that is, the deliberate and conscious abandonment of outdated beliefs, mental models and practices, makes the reconstruction of knowledge absolutely superficial and thus, algorithmically condescending interaction does not produce deep and authentic knowledge, regardless of AI Augmentation Intensity.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Most biographies follow a life through time. This one follows a life through an equation. Satish Gajawada, an Integrated Dual Degree (B.Tech + M.Tech) graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee (2012), has spent fourteen years as an independent researcher who gives names, structure and heart to ideas in artificial intelligence: Excellent AI (EAI), Very Highly Advanced AI (VHAAI), Out of the Box AI (OBAI), a society (ISVHAAI), a family of value-themed swarm algorithms, thirteen theories of human purpose, a 108-right taxonomy of human rights, and a lifelong “thesis” supervised by his parents and GOD. Reading the particle swarm update rule as a metaphor for a research life, this article identifies four forces (inertia, personal best, global best and exploration) and one outcome: a position update that, in 2026, turned decisively toward testing and open disclosure. Drawing on eight source documents, with each statement attributed to a published work, a manuscript or the subject’s own account, we show that a reproducible genetic-algorithm and PSO experiment found a fairness weight that cut a demographic-parity gap from 0.121 to 0.016 for 1.9 points of accuracy, and a gentler weight that improved accuracy and fairness together. Itemised output rose from one entry in 2012 to twelve in 2026. We conclude that Gajawada is a builder of human-centred vocabulary and institutions, a grateful son, a joyful experimenter and a candid author, and that his life offers every learner a portable update rule: keep your direction, honour your best, listen to your guides, stay curious, and keep moving.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study has explored the influence of speaking anxiety as a major obstacle for English as foreign language learners (EFL) in their non-native environment like in the private universities in Dhaka, Bangladesh. With the up rise of Artificial Intelligence, English language learning applications have incorporated AI-based features to enhance the learning experience. This finding examined how AI-supported speaking apps, in this instance, Duolingo and ELSA Speak, reduce speaking anxiety and increase learners' confidence, fluency and speaking skills through AI-driven personalized feedback, gamified interaction and adaptive learning. This research used mixed-method approach, which included qualitative and quantitative methods to provide comprehensive insights and understanding. The results of the study pointed to the effectiveness of AI-based language learning apps in creating a supportive language-learning atmosphere, enhancing the learning process and reducing stress levels when practicing oral communication. The results of this study could contribute to the understanding of how AI-based app-based learning can be incorporated in the university curriculum and evidence-based recommendations for teachers, educational technology designers and policy makers.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing Englishlanguage learning by providing personalized instruction, immediate feedback,interactive communication, and opportunities for independent practice. This paperexamines the potential benefits and challenges of integrating AI technologies intoEnglish as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning. The study adopts a literature reviewapproach and draws on existing empirical research, systematic reviews, andinternational educational guidance. The reviewed literature suggests that AI-supportedlearning can contribute to language development, particularly by providing writingfeedback, facilitating conversational practice, and supporting learner engagement.However, the effectiveness of these technologies depends on the quality of AIgenerated feedback, learners’ digital literacy, appropriate pedagogical guidance, andresponsible use. Potential challenges include inaccurate information, excessivedependence on AI, academic integrity concerns, and data privacy risks. The paperargues that AI should complement rather than replace teachers and meaningful humaninteraction. It concludes that the responsible integration of AI into English languageeducation requires clear learning objectives, critical evaluation of AI-generated content,and a balanced combination of technological tools and teacher-led instruction.

OBJECTIVE: Individualized rehabilitation plans are crucial for maximizing clinical outcomes. Generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), which can generate new content based on large knowledge bases, could improve personalized rehabilitation. This systematic review aimed to assess accuracy and application of LLMs in rehabilitation. DESIGN: A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus until February 2026. The PICO included LLMs (P), their use in rehabilitation planning (I), comparison with expert opinion or other AI systems (e.g., machine learning, deep learning, or CDSS) (C), the ability to generate appropriate rehabilitation plans and compliance with expert clinicians or clinical practice guidelines (O). Studies involving non-generative AI were excluded. Methodological quality was assessed with JBI tools. Data extraction was performed by two reviewers; a third resolved conflicts. RESULTS: Nine studies met inclusion criteria. Concordance with expert opinion varied, reaching 98.75% after an expert advisory board reviewed AI-generated statements. In musculoskeletal and cardiovascular rehabilitation, LLMs demonstrated alignment with guidelines. However, the included studies reported hallucinations, underscoring the necessity of supervision. CONCLUSION: LLMs showed promising capabilities in supporting rehabilitation treatment planning, possibly offering adaptability and personalization. Nonetheless, high-quality studies are necessary to validate real-world effectiveness and define implementation strategies.
